chapters.title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XLI
paragraphs:
Blustering never helped me prosper,
For the rain comes down every day.
—_Twelfth Night_.
The dealings Caleb Garth had mentioned between Mr. Bulstrode and Mr. Joshua Rigg Featherstone over the land belonging to Stone Court had led the two men to exchange a letter or two.

Who can say what writing may bring about? Words carved in stone may lie face down for centuries on a deserted beach, or “rest quietly under the drums and tramplings of many conquests,” and finally reveal the secrets of stolen power and other scandals that were gossip in long-vanished empires. The world seems to be one enormous whispering gallery. Our little lifetimes often reproduce these circumstances in miniature. A stone kicked about by generations of country fools may, through a curious chain of small events, come to a scholar's notice. His work may eventually make it the means of dating invasions and unlocking the mysteries of religions. In the same way, a scrap of ink-covered paper, long used innocently as wrapping or to plug a gap, may at last unfold before the one pair of eyes whose knowledge can turn it into the beginning of a catastrophe. To Uriel, watching the history of the planets from the sun, either result would be equally coincidental.

After that rather elevated comparison, I feel less embarrassed about drawing attention to low people. However little we like their interference, they do a great deal to determine the world's course. Certainly it would be good if we could reduce their numbers; perhaps we might do something by being less careless about bringing them into existence. In social terms, most people would have called Joshua Rigg unnecessary. But people like Peter Featherstone, whom nobody ever asked to reproduce themselves, are the very last to wait for a request, in prose or verse. In this instance the copy took more of its outward appearance from the mother. In a woman, frog-like features, combined with rosy cheeks and a rounded figure, can have considerable charm for certain admirers. The result is sometimes a frog-faced man, surely desirable to no class of intelligent beings. Especially when he suddenly appears to defeat other people's expectations—the worst possible way for a socially unnecessary person to present himself.

Yet Mr. Rigg Featherstone's low qualities were entirely of the sober, water-drinking sort. From morning until night he was as sleek, tidy and cool as the frog he resembled. Old Peter had secretly chuckled over a son almost more calculating than himself and far harder to disturb. I should add that he looked after his fingernails meticulously, and intended to marry a well-educated young woman, not yet selected, who was good-looking and had indisputably respectable middle-class connections. His nails and his modest ambitions thus compared well with those of most gentlemen, although his ambitions had been shaped only by his opportunities as a clerk and accountant in the smaller businesses of a port town. He thought the country Featherstones absurdly simple people. For their part, they considered his upbringing in a seaport a further aggravation of the monstrous fact that their brother Peter—and, still more, Peter's property—should have such connections.

Seen from the two windows of Stone Court's panelled sitting room, the garden and gravel drive had never looked neater. Mr. Rigg Featherstone stood gazing out at them with his hands behind his back, their owner now. It was uncertain, though, whether he wanted to contemplate his grounds or merely turn his back on the person standing in the middle of the room, legs wide apart and hands in his trouser pockets. In every respect this visitor contrasted with the sleek, cool Rigg. Plainly approaching sixty, he was red-faced and hairy, with plenty of grey in his bushy whiskers and thick curls. His rather stout body made the worn seams of his clothes more conspicuous. He had the manner of a swaggering man determined to attract attention even at a fireworks display, convinced that his comments on someone else's performance would interest people more than the performance itself.

His name was John Raffles. He sometimes jokingly added W.A.G. to his signature, explaining that he had once been taught by Leonard Lamb of Finsbury, who put B.A. after his name. It was he, Raffles, who had thought up the joke of calling that celebrated headmaster Ba-Lamb. Such were Mr. Raffles's looks and turn of mind. Both seemed to carry the stale smell of the commercial travellers' rooms in the hotels of that time.
“Come along, Josh,” he was saying in a deep, rumbling voice. “Think of it this way: your poor mother's getting on in years, and now you could afford to give her a decent sum to make her comfortable.”
“Not while you're alive. She'll never be comfortable as long as you live,” Rigg answered in his cool, high voice. “Whatever I give her, you'll take.”

“You've got a grudge against me, Josh. I know that. But come on—man to man, no nonsense—a little money to start with could help me make a first-rate business of the shop. The tobacco trade's growing. I'd be cutting off my nose to spite my face if I didn't make the most of it. For my own sake, I'd stick to it like a flea to a fleece. I'd always be there. And nothing would please your poor mother more. I've about finished sowing my wild oats—I'm past fifty-five. I want to settle down by my own fireside. Once I put my back into the tobacco business, I could bring brains and experience to it that you wouldn't easily find anywhere else. I don't want to keep troubling you. I want to get everything on the right track once and for all. Think about it, Josh—man to man—and think of your poor mother, comfortable for the rest of her life. I've always been fond of the old woman, by Jove!”
“Finished?” Mr. Rigg asked quietly, still facing the window.
“Yes, _I've_ finished,” said Raffles. He took hold of his hat on the table before him and pushed it forward as though concluding a speech.

“Then listen. The more often you say something, the less I'll believe it. The more you want me to do something, the stronger my reason never to do it. Do you imagine I'll forget how you kicked me when I was a boy, and took all the best food from me and my mother? Do you think I've forgotten how you kept coming home, selling everything, pocketing the money and leaving us helpless again? I'd be glad to see you whipped behind a cart. My mother was a fool where you were concerned. She had no right to give me a stepfather, and she's paid for it. She'll get her weekly allowance, and nothing more. And even that will stop if you dare set foot on this property again, or follow me into this part of the country. Next time you come through those gates, the dogs and the wagon driver's whip will drive you out.”

At these last words, Rigg turned and fixed his bulging, icy eyes on Raffles. The contrast between them was as sharp as it could have been eighteen years earlier, when Rigg was an unappealing boy who invited a kick and Raffles the rather stocky Adonis of bars and back rooms. But Rigg now had the advantage. Anyone overhearing them might have expected Raffles to slink away like a beaten dog. Nothing of the sort. He made the face he habitually made when he lost at a game, then relaxed into a laugh and pulled a brandy flask from his pocket.
“Come on, Josh,” he coaxed. “Give me a drop of brandy and a sovereign for the journey home, and I'll be off. On my honour! I'll go like a bullet, _by_ Jove!”

“Understand this,” said Rigg, taking out a bunch of keys. “If I see you again, I won't speak to you. I acknowledge no more connection with you than with a crow. And if you claim a connection with me, all you'll gain is a reputation for what you are—a spiteful, brazen, bullying scoundrel.”

“Well, that's a pity, Josh,” said Raffles, pretending to scratch his head and raise his brows in bewilderment. “I'm very fond of you. _By_ Jove, I am! I like nothing better than tormenting you—you're so like your mother—and now I must give it up. But we have a bargain about the brandy and the sovereign.”

He thrust the flask forward, and Rigg took his keys to a fine old oak bureau. The movement had reminded Raffles that the flask was dangerously loose in its leather case. He noticed a folded paper lying inside the fireplace guard, picked it up and pushed it under the leather to hold the glass firmly in place.

By then Rigg had returned with a brandy bottle. He filled the flask and handed over a sovereign, without either looking at Raffles or speaking. After locking the bureau again, he went back to the window and stared out as expressionlessly as at the beginning of the visit. Meanwhile Raffles took a little drink, screwed the flask shut and tucked it into his side pocket with deliberately irritating slowness, making a face behind his stepson's back.
“Farewell, Josh—and if for ever!” Raffles said, looking back as he opened the door.

Rigg watched him cross the grounds and turn into the lane. The grey day had developed into a light drizzle. It freshened the hedges and grassy edges of the side roads, and hurried the labourers loading the last bundles of grain. Raffles walked with the awkward gait of a town loafer forced to travel a stretch of country on foot. Amid the damp countryside's quiet and industry, he looked as out of place as a baboon escaped from a menagerie. But only calves long past weaning stared at him, and only the little water rats, scurrying away as he approached, showed any dislike of his appearance.

On reaching the main road he had the good luck to be overtaken by a stagecoach, which took him to Brassing. There he boarded the recently built railway, remarking to the other passengers that he thought it had been properly broken in now that it had killed Huskisson. On most occasions Mr. Raffles maintained his sense of having been educated at an academy and of being able, if he chose, to pass muster anywhere. Indeed, he never met a fellow human being whom he did not feel entitled to ridicule and torment, quite sure that everyone else present would enjoy the entertainment.

He performed that role now as cheerfully as if his journey had been a complete success, taking frequent drinks from his flask. The paper wedged around it was a letter signed _Nicholas Bulstrode_. But Raffles was unlikely to disturb it while it was serving its present useful purpose.

chapters.title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XLII
paragraphs:
How deeply I could scorn this man,
If charity did not forbid it!
—SHAKESPEARE: _Henry VIII_.
Soon after returning from his honeymoon, Lydgate made a professional visit to Lowick Manor. A letter had asked him to arrange a time to call.

Mr. Casaubon had never questioned Lydgate about the nature of his illness. Even to Dorothea he had shown no anxiety about how much it might shorten either his work or his life. On this subject, as on every other, he recoiled from pity. The suspicion that people pitied some aspect of his circumstances which they had guessed or discovered against his wishes was bitter enough. The thought of inviting an expression of sympathy by openly admitting fear or sorrow was therefore unbearable. Every proud person knows something of this feeling. Perhaps only a sense of fellowship deep enough to make every attempt at isolation seem small and mean, rather than noble, can overcome it.

But something now occupied Mr. Casaubon's thoughts that made the question of his health and life haunt his silences even more insistently than his writing, still unripe in the autumn of his years. Certainly that work could be called his central ambition. Yet in some kinds of authorship the chief product is the painful sensitivity accumulated in the author's mind. One knows the river is there only by a few streaks of water amid a vast deposit of unpleasant mud. That was the case with Mr. Casaubon's exhausting intellectual labours. Their most distinctive result was not the “Key to All Mythologies.” It was his unhealthy awareness that others denied him a standing he had never demonstrably earned; his constant suspicion that their opinions of him were unfavourable; the sad absence of passion from his efforts to achieve something, and his passionate refusal to admit that he had achieved nothing.

So the intellectual ambition that seemed to others to have consumed and dried him up offered no protection against injury, least of all injury from Dorothea. And now he had begun imagining possibilities for the future that somehow embittered him more than anything he had considered before.

Certain facts were beyond his power to alter. There was Will Ladislaw's existence, his defiant determination to remain near Lowick, and his frivolous attitude towards the possessors of genuine, certified learning. There was Dorothea's nature, always finding some new form of eager activity, and concealing even beneath submission and silence passionate reasons which it was irritating to contemplate. There were the opinions and sympathies that had taken hold of her on subjects he could not possibly discuss with her. He could not deny that Dorothea was as virtuous and lovely a young wife as he could have found. But a young wife proved more troublesome than he had imagined. She nursed him, read to him, anticipated his needs and worried about his feelings. Nevertheless, he had become certain that she judged him. Her wifely devotion seemed an act of penance for disbelieving thoughts. Along with it came a capacity for comparison that placed him and his work in an all too revealing light among things in general. Like vapour, his discontent passed through every gentle expression of her love and clung to the unappreciative world which she had merely brought closer to him.

Poor Mr. Casaubon! His suffering was harder to bear because it felt like betrayal. The young creature who had worshipped him with complete confidence had soon become a critical wife. Her early criticisms and expressions of resentment had left an impression no later tenderness or obedience could erase. His suspicious mind now read her silence as rebellion held in check. An unexpected remark asserted her awareness of her own superiority. Her gentle answers were irritatingly cautious; when she agreed, she was congratulating herself on her patience. The harder he struggled to hide this inner drama, the more vividly he experienced it, just as we hear more acutely a sound we hope nobody else will hear.

Far from finding Mr. Casaubon's resulting misery surprising, I think it quite ordinary. Cannot a tiny speck held close to our eyes blot out the world's splendour, leaving only a rim of light by which to see the obstruction? I know no speck more troublesome than the self. And if Mr. Casaubon had chosen to explain his grievances—his suspicion that he was no longer adored without criticism—who could have denied that he had good grounds? Indeed, there was a powerful reason to add which he had not explicitly considered: he was not entirely adorable. He suspected this, however, as he suspected other things without admitting them. Like the rest of us, he felt how comforting it would be to have a companion who would never discover the fact.

This painful sensitivity towards Dorothea was fully established before Will Ladislaw returned to Lowick. Events since then had driven Mr. Casaubon's talent for suspicious interpretation into furious activity. To the facts he knew, he added imaginary facts about the present and future. These became more real to him than the actual ones, because they aroused stronger dislike and a more overwhelming bitterness. Suspicion and jealousy kept weaving their web around Will Ladislaw's intentions and Dorothea's impressions. It would be quite unfair to suppose that he could have put any vulgar interpretation on Dorothea's conduct. His own habits of thought and behaviour, as much as the obvious nobility of her nature, protected him from that mistake. What he jealously guarded was her opinion: the influence that might guide her passionate judgments, and the future possibilities towards which they might lead her. Until Will's last defiant letter, he had had no definite charge he would choose to bring formally against him. Still, he felt justified in believing Will capable of any scheme that might appeal to a rebellious nature and uncontrolled impulses. He was certain Dorothea had caused Will's return from Rome and his decision to settle nearby. He was perceptive enough to imagine that she had innocently encouraged it. Clearly she was ready to become attached to Will and to yield to his suggestions. They had never talked alone without her coming away with some new, troublesome idea. The last such meeting that Mr. Casaubon knew about had led to a scene that made him angrier with them both than ever before. On returning from Freshitt Hall, Dorothea had for the first time said nothing about seeing Will. Her flood of ideas about money, poured out in the darkness of the night, had only introduced a mixture of still more hateful fears into her husband's mind.

And the recent blow to his health was always painfully with him. Certainly he felt much better. His usual capacity for work had returned. Perhaps the illness had been only exhaustion, and twenty years of achievement still lay ahead to justify thirty years of preparation. That prospect was sweetened by a taste of revenge upon the premature sneers of Carp and company. Even as Mr. Casaubon carried his little candle among the tombs of the past, those modern figures crossed its dim light and interrupted his patient exploration. To prove Carp wrong, forcing him to swallow his words with considerable indigestion, would be a pleasant incidental reward of literary triumph. The prospect of surviving through future ages on earth and for all eternity in heaven did not prevent him from dwelling on it. Since the expectation of his own endless bliss could not remove the bitter flavours of jealousy and revenge, it is less surprising that the likelihood of other people's brief earthly happiness after he had entered glory did little to sweeten his temper. If a disease really was undermining him, some people might have considerable opportunity to be happier once he was gone. If one of those people were Will Ladislaw, Mr. Casaubon objected so strongly that his resentment seemed likely to accompany him into a disembodied existence.

This states the case very baldly, and therefore very incompletely. The human soul runs in many channels. As we know, Mr. Casaubon had a sense of right and an honourable pride in fulfilling the demands of honour. These obliged him to find motives for his conduct other than jealousy and revenge. He put the case to himself like this: “When I married Dorothea Brooke, I undertook to provide for her welfare after my death. But ample property held independently does not guarantee welfare. On the contrary, circumstances could make such possessions a danger to her. Any man skilful enough to exploit either her passionate affections or her quixotic enthusiasm would find her easy prey. And there is a man here who intends exactly that—a man governed only by passing whims, and personally hostile to me. Of that I am certain. His hostility feeds on his awareness of his own ingratitude, and he has repeatedly expressed it by ridiculing me. I am as sure of this as if I had heard him. Even if I live, I shall worry about what he may try to accomplish by indirect influence. He has won Dorothea's ear and fascinated her. He has plainly tried to persuade her that he has claims on me beyond anything I have done for him. If I die—and he is staying here to watch for that—he will persuade her to marry him. It would be a disaster for her and a triumph for him. _She_ would not see the disaster. He could make her believe anything. She is inclined to excessive attachment, and secretly blames me for failing to respond to it. Already she is preoccupied with his fortunes. He imagines an easy conquest, and taking over my nest. I will prevent that! Such a marriage would ruin Dorothea. Has he ever persevered in anything except out of opposition? In learning he has always wanted an impressive show for little effort. In religion, he could easily echo Dorothea's peculiar ideas for as long as it suited him. When has shallow learning ever been separate from loose principles? I distrust his morals completely. It is my duty to do everything I can to prevent his plans succeeding.”

The arrangements Mr. Casaubon had made at his marriage left him free to take strong measures. But considering those measures inevitably made him dwell on his own chances of survival. At last his desire for the most accurate possible estimate overcame his proud reserve. He resolved to ask Lydgate what his illness was.

He told Dorothea that Lydgate had an appointment to visit at half past three. When she anxiously asked whether he had felt ill, he answered, “No. I merely wish to consult him about some recurring symptoms. You need not see him, my dear. I shall arrange for him to join me in the Yew-tree Walk, where I shall be taking my customary exercise.”

Entering the Yew-tree Walk, Lydgate saw Mr. Casaubon moving slowly away, his head bowed and his hands, as usual, behind his back. The afternoon was beautiful. Leaves from the tall lime trees drifted silently across the sombre evergreens; light and shadow lay sleeping side by side. Nothing broke the silence except the cawing of rooks, a lullaby to an accustomed ear—or that last, solemn lullaby, a funeral song. Lydgate, conscious of his own vigorous body in its prime, felt some pity as the figure he was about to overtake turned towards him. Coming closer, it displayed the signs of premature age more plainly than ever: a scholar's stooping shoulders, wasted limbs, and melancholy lines around the mouth. “Poor man,” he thought. “Some men of his age are like lions. You can tell nothing about their age except that they're fully grown.”
“Mr. Lydgate,” said Mr. Casaubon with his unfailing politeness, “I am most grateful for your punctuality. If you please, we shall talk as we walk up and down.”
“I hope you haven't asked me here because the unpleasant symptoms have returned,” said Lydgate, breaking a silence.

“Not directly—no. To explain my request, I must mention something that would otherwise need no reference. My life, insignificant in every other respect, may have some importance because the work that has occupied all its best years remains incomplete. In brief, I have long been engaged on a work I should wish to leave at least sufficiently advanced for publication by—others. If I knew that this was all I could reasonably hope for, such knowledge would usefully limit my efforts. It would guide me both in deciding what to undertake and what to set aside.”

Here Mr. Casaubon stopped. He brought one hand from behind his back and slipped it between the buttons of his single-breasted coat. To anyone with a deep understanding of human destiny, few things could have been more compelling than the inner conflict suggested by this formal, measured speech, delivered in his usual singsong, with the familiar movement of his head. Indeed, what could be more sublimely tragic than a soul struggling with the demand to abandon the work that has given its whole life meaning—a meaning destined to vanish like waters that come and go where nobody needs them? But nothing about Mr. Casaubon struck others as sublime. Lydgate, ready with a certain contempt for useless scholarship, felt a little amusement mingle with his pity. He knew too little of disaster yet to understand the pathos of a life in which everything fell below the level of tragedy except the sufferer's passionate self-concern.
“You mean the obstacles that poor health might put in your way?” he asked, trying to help Mr. Casaubon towards the point some hesitation seemed to be obstructing.

“I do. You have not suggested to me that the symptoms you observed with such painstaking care—which I must acknowledge—indicated a fatal illness. But if they did, Mr. Lydgate, I should wish to know the entire truth. I ask you to state your conclusions precisely, as a service of friendship. If you can tell me that nothing threatens my life beyond its ordinary accidents, I shall rejoice, for the reasons I have given. If you cannot, then knowing the truth matters still more to me.”

“Then I need no longer hesitate about what to do,” said Lydgate. “But first I must make you understand that my conclusions are uncertain for two reasons. I can make mistakes, and heart disease is particularly difficult to predict. In any event, it is scarcely possible to add much to life's already enormous uncertainty.”
Mr. Casaubon visibly flinched, but bowed.

“I believe you have what is called fatty degeneration of the heart. Laennec, who gave us the stethoscope not many years ago, first recognised and investigated the disease. We still need much more experience and longer observation of it. But after what you have said, I have a duty to tell you that it often causes sudden death. At the same time, that outcome cannot be predicted. Your condition might allow you another fifteen years of reasonably comfortable life, or even longer. Anything more I could tell you would consist of anatomical or medical details, leaving your expectations exactly where they are.” Lydgate was perceptive enough to know that Mr. Casaubon would take plain speech, without a show of excessive caution, as a mark of respect.
“Thank you, Mr. Lydgate,” said Mr. Casaubon after a brief pause. “There is one more question. Have you told Mrs. Casaubon what you have just told me?”

“In part—that is, about the possible outcomes.” Lydgate was about to explain why he had spoken to Dorothea, but Mr. Casaubon gave a slight wave of his hand, unmistakably wishing to end the conversation. He repeated, “Thank you,” and began commenting on the day's exceptional beauty.

Lydgate, sure that his patient wanted solitude, soon left. The dark figure continued pacing, hands behind his back and head bowed. The sombre yews offered silent companionship to his melancholy. Little shadows of birds or leaves flitted across the islands of sunlight, moving soundlessly as though in the presence of grief. Here was a man looking into death's eyes for the first time. He was passing through one of those rare moments when we feel the truth of a commonplace. That differs from what we call knowing it as much as the sight of water on the earth differs from the feverish vision of water that cannot be reached to cool a burning tongue. When “We must all die” suddenly becomes the sharp awareness “I must die—and soon,” death seizes us, and his fingers are cruel. Later he may gather us into his arms as our mother did, and our last dim moment of earthly awareness may resemble our first. Mr. Casaubon now felt as if he had suddenly arrived at the bank of the dark river and heard the splash of an approaching oar. He could distinguish no figures, but waited to be summoned. At such a time the mind does not abandon its lifelong inclination. Imagination carries that inclination beyond death and looks back, perhaps with the divine calm of generosity, perhaps with the petty anxieties of self-assertion. Mr. Casaubon's actions will give us a clue to his inclination. With certain private scholarly reservations, he considered himself a believing Christian, both in his judgments of the present and his hopes for the future. Yet what we seek to satisfy, even when we call it a distant hope, is a present desire. The future estate for which men toil in city alleys already exists in their love and imagination. Mr. Casaubon's present longing was not for divine fellowship and light free of earthly conditions. Poor man, his passionate desires clung close to the ground like mist in deeply shaded places.

Dorothea knew when Lydgate rode away. She stepped into the garden, her first impulse to go straight to her husband. But she hesitated, afraid of offending him by intruding. Her warmth, repeatedly rebuffed, combined with her intense memory to deepen her fear, as frustrated energy sinks into a shudder. She wandered slowly around the nearest groups of trees until she saw him coming. Then she moved towards him. She might have been an angel sent from heaven to promise that the few hours left would still be filled with faithful love—a love that held more closely now it understood his grief. His answering glance was so cold that her timidity increased. Even so, she turned beside him and slipped her hand through his arm.
Mr. Casaubon left his hands behind his back, letting her supple arm cling awkwardly to his stiff one.

The feeling this hard, unresponsive arm gave Dorothea was horrible. That is a strong word, but not too strong. Through acts we call trivial, the seeds of joy are continually squandered. Finally men and women look with haggard faces at the devastation their own waste has created and declare that the earth yields no sweetness, calling their denial knowledge. You may ask how Mr. Casaubon could behave like this and call himself a man. Remember that his mind recoiled from pity. Have you ever watched what happens to such a mind when it suspects that its own grief may bring satisfaction, now or later, to the very person whose pity already offends it? Besides, he understood little of Dorothea's feelings. It had not occurred to him that on this occasion they could be as strong as his own feelings about Carp's criticisms.

Dorothea kept her arm where it was, but dared not speak. Mr. Casaubon did not tell her, “I want to be alone.” He simply walked towards the house in silence. As they entered through the glass door on the east side, she withdrew her arm and stayed behind on the matting to leave him entirely free. He went into the library and shut himself in with his sorrow.

She went upstairs to her sitting room. Through the open bow window came the afternoon's tranquil splendour over the avenue, where the lime trees cast long shadows. But Dorothea saw none of it. She flung herself into a chair, unaware that dazzling sunlight fell on her. If it caused discomfort, how could she distinguish it from her inward misery?
She was swept up in a rebellious anger stronger than any she had known since marrying. Words came instead of tears:
“What have I done—what am I—to deserve this treatment? He never understands what's in my mind. He never cares. What good is anything I do? He wishes he had never married me.”

Hearing her own voice, she stopped and grew still. Like someone exhausted and lost, she sat seeing in a single glance every path her youthful hopes had taken, paths she could never find again. In the same miserable light she saw clearly her own loneliness and her husband's. They walked so far apart that she was forced to look at him from a distance. Had he drawn her close, she would never have examined him, never asked, “Is he worth living for?” She would simply have felt him part of her own life. Now she said bitterly, “The fault is his, not mine.” The shock through her whole being had overthrown pity. Was she to blame for believing in him, believing him worthy? And what exactly was he? She was quite capable of judging him—she who trembled as she watched for his glances, who imprisoned her best self and visited it only in secret so that she might become small enough to please him. In a crisis like this, some women begin to hate.

The sun was low when Dorothea decided she would not go down again. She would send word to her husband that she felt unwell and preferred to stay upstairs. Never before had she deliberately let resentment rule her this way. But now she believed she could not face him without telling him the truth about her feelings, and she must wait until she could speak without interruption. Her message might puzzle and hurt him. It was good that he should be puzzled and hurt. Her anger told her, as anger so often does, that God was on her side. All heaven, even if crowded with spirits watching them, must take her part. She had decided to ring the bell when someone knocked at the door.
Mr. Casaubon had sent word that he would dine in the library. He was very busy and wished to spend the evening entirely alone.
“Then I won't have dinner, Tantripp.”
“Oh, madam, won't you let me bring you a little something?”
“No, I feel ill. Please make everything ready in my dressing room, but don't disturb me again.”

Dorothea sat almost without moving through her inward struggle as evening slowly became night. Yet the struggle kept changing, like that of a man who first moves to strike someone and ends by mastering the desire to strike. Committing a crime requires no more energy than a determined act of submission when the soul's noble habits regain their strength. The thought that had taken Dorothea out to meet her husband could not stay away for long. She was convinced he had been asking whether all his work might soon be stopped, and that the answer must have pierced his heart. That conviction rose beside her image of him like a dim, admonishing figure, sadly reproaching her anger. It cost her a litany of imagined sorrows and silent cries that she might become the mercy those sorrows needed. But at last she resolved to yield. When the house was quiet and she knew it was nearly his usual bedtime, she gently opened her door. She stood outside in the dark, waiting for him to come upstairs with his light. If he did not come soon, she thought, she would go down and risk another wound. She would never again expect anything else. Then she heard the library door open. Slowly the light rose up the stairs, the carpet muffling his footsteps. When he stood opposite her, she saw how much more drawn his face had become. He gave a little start at seeing her. Without speaking, she looked up at him imploringly.
“Dorothea!” he said, gently surprised. “Have you been waiting for me?”
“Yes. I didn't want to interrupt you.”
“Come, my dear. You're young; you needn't lengthen your life by staying awake.”

The quiet, sorrowful kindness of those words brought Dorothea something like the gratitude we might feel after narrowly avoiding an injury to a helpless, wounded creature. She placed her hand in her husband's, and together they walked along the wide corridor.

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLIII
paragraphs:
“This figure is expensive: carved with love
Long centuries ago in finest ivory.
No passing fashion here, but pure, proud lines
Of generous womanhood for every age.
That piece is costly too: painted earthenware,
Cleverly fashioned for a nobleman's eye.
The smile, you see, is perfect—marvellous
For mere glazed clay! An ornament to grace
The richest setting on a table.”

Dorothea rarely went out without her husband. Occasionally, though, she drove alone into Middlemarch on the small shopping or charitable errands that fall to any comfortably wealthy woman living within three miles of a town. Two days after the scene in the Yew-tree Walk, she decided to use one of these opportunities to see Lydgate if she could. She wanted to learn whether her husband had felt some discouraging change in his symptoms which he was hiding from her, and whether he had insisted on hearing the full truth about his condition. Asking someone else for information about him made her feel almost guilty. But the fear of not knowing—of an ignorance that might make her harsh or unjust—overcame her scruples. She was certain he had passed through some inner crisis. The very next day he had begun rearranging his notes by a new method and given her a quite new role in carrying out his plan. Poor Dorothea needed to store up patience.
It was about four when she reached Lydgate's house in Lowick Gate. Suddenly doubtful that he would be home, she wished she had written first. He was indeed out.
“Is Mrs. Lydgate at home?” asked Dorothea. So far as she knew, she had never seen Rosamond, but now remembered the marriage. Yes, Mrs. Lydgate was in.
“Then I'll come in and speak to her, if she doesn't mind. Would you ask whether she can see me—Mrs. Casaubon—for a few minutes?”

While the servant carried her message inside, Dorothea heard music through an open window: a few notes sung by a man, followed by a burst of elaborate runs on the piano. The runs stopped abruptly. Then the servant returned to say that Mrs. Lydgate would be pleased to receive Mrs. Casaubon.

When the drawing-room door opened and Dorothea came in, she created a contrast often seen in country life when the habits of different social ranks were less mixed than they are today. Those who know such things must tell us the exact name of the fabric she wore that mild autumn: a thin white wool, soft to the touch and to the eye. It always seemed freshly washed, scented with sweet hedges. It was always made into a long coat whose hanging sleeves were entirely out of fashion. Yet if she had appeared before a hushed audience as Imogen or Cato's daughter, her clothes might have seemed perfectly appropriate. Grace and dignity lived in her limbs and neck. Around her simply parted hair and candid eyes, the large round poke bonnet then imposed on women looked no stranger than the golden plate we call a halo. No dramatic heroine could have aroused more interest than Mrs. Casaubon in the two people now watching her. To Rosamond she was one of the county divinities who did not mingle with Middlemarch mortals, and whose smallest details of dress or manner deserved study. Rosamond was also pleased that Mrs. Casaubon would have an opportunity to study _her_. What was the use of being exquisite unless the best judges saw you? Since receiving the highest compliments at Sir Godwin Lydgate's, she felt entirely confident of the impression she would make on people of good birth. Dorothea offered her hand with her usual unaffected kindness and looked admiringly at Lydgate's lovely bride. She was aware of a gentleman some distance away, but saw him only as a coated figure at the edge of her vision. He was too absorbed in the presence of one woman to consider the contrast between the two, though it would certainly have struck an untroubled observer. Both were tall, their eyes on the same level. But picture Rosamond's childlike fairness and magnificent crown of braids, her pale blue dress so perfectly cut and fashionable that no dressmaker could view it unmoved. Add the large embroidered collar, whose price one hoped every spectator would appreciate, the rings carefully displaying her little hands, and the restrained awareness of herself which is the costly substitute for simplicity.

“Thank you for letting me interrupt you,” Dorothea said at once. “I'm anxious to see Mr. Lydgate before I go home, if I can. I hoped you might tell me where to find him, or perhaps let me wait if you expect him back soon.”
“He's at the New Hospital,” Rosamond replied. “I don't know when he'll be back, but I can send for him.”

“Will you let me fetch him?” Will Ladislaw asked, stepping forward. He had picked up his hat before Dorothea came in. She flushed in surprise, but held out her hand with an unmistakably delighted smile.
“I didn't realise it was you. I never expected to find you here.”
“Shall I go to the Hospital and tell Mr. Lydgate you'd like to see him?” Will asked.
“It would be quicker to send my carriage,” said Dorothea, “if you'd be so kind as to give the coachman the message.”

Will was going towards the door when a whole chain of connected memories flashed through Dorothea's mind. Turning quickly, she said, “Thank you, but I'll go myself. I don't want to lose any time before returning home. I'll drive to the Hospital and see Mr. Lydgate there. Please forgive me, Mrs. Lydgate. I'm very grateful to you.”

Some sudden thought had clearly seized her attention. She left almost unaware of her immediate surroundings, scarcely noticing that Will opened the door and offered his arm to take her to the carriage. She accepted his arm but said nothing. Will felt rather hurt and miserable, and could find nothing to say either. He helped her silently into the carriage. They said goodbye, and she drove off.

During the five-minute journey to the Hospital, thoughts entirely new to her came into her mind. Her decision to leave, and her distraction as she left, arose from a sudden feeling that deliberately allowing further contact with Will would be a kind of deception if she could not mention it to her husband. Already she was concealing her purpose in seeking Lydgate. This was all she had consciously thought, but a vague uneasiness had also driven her. Now, alone in the carriage, she heard again in her mind the man's singing and accompanying piano, which she had barely noticed before. With some surprise, she found herself considering that Will Ladislaw was spending time with Mrs. Lydgate while her husband was out. Then she could not help remembering that he had spent time with her in similar circumstances. Why should that be improper? But Will was Mr. Casaubon's relation, someone she had a duty to treat kindly. Still, perhaps there had been signs she ought to have understood: signs that Mr. Casaubon disliked his cousin's visits during his own absence. “Perhaps I've been wrong about many things,” poor Dorothea told herself, as tears rolled down her cheeks and had to be wiped away quickly. Her unhappiness was confused. The image of Will, once so clear to her, had been mysteriously spoiled. Then the carriage stopped at the Hospital gate. Soon she was walking around the lawns with Lydgate, and her feelings returned to the urgent purpose that had brought her there.

Meanwhile, Will Ladislaw felt humiliated and knew exactly why. His opportunities to see Dorothea were rare. Now, for the first time, one of them had put him at a disadvantage. Previously the difficulty had simply been that he was not her chief concern. Now she had seen him in circumstances suggesting that she might not be his. He felt pushed farther away from her, into the circles of Middlemarch society that formed no part of her life. Yet that was not his fault. Naturally, since taking lodgings in town, he had made as many acquaintances as possible: his position required him to know everyone and everything. Lydgate was worth knowing more than anyone else nearby, and happened to have a musical wife well worth visiting. That was the entire explanation of the situation in which Diana had descended too unexpectedly upon her worshipper. It was humiliating. Will knew he would never have been in Middlemarch without Dorothea. Yet his position there now threatened to separate him from her by barriers of habitual feeling more destructive of mutual interest than the entire distance between Rome and Britain. Prejudices about rank and status were easy to defy when embodied in a tyrannical letter from Mr. Casaubon. But prejudices, like fragrant objects, exist in two forms, solid and intangible: solid as the pyramids, subtle as the twentieth echo of an echo, or the memory of hyacinths that once perfumed the dark. Will's temperament made him acutely aware of these subtleties. A less perceptive man would not have sensed, as he did, that Dorothea had for the first time felt something improper in being entirely at ease with him, and that a chill had entered their silence as he took her to the carriage. Perhaps Casaubon, in his jealous hatred, had been insisting that Will had fallen beneath her socially. Damn Casaubon!
Will went back into the drawing room and picked up his hat. Looking annoyed, he approached Mrs. Lydgate, who was now sitting at her worktable, and said:
“Interrupting music or poetry is always fatal. May I come another day to finish what we were saying about performing ‘Lungi dal caro bene’?”

“I should be delighted with the lesson,” said Rosamond. “But surely you agree that this was a very beautiful interruption. I quite envy you knowing Mrs. Casaubon. Is she very intelligent? She looks as though she is.”
“Honestly, I've never considered it,” Will answered sulkily.
“Tertius gave exactly that answer when I first asked whether she was beautiful. What do you gentlemen think about when you're with Mrs. Casaubon?”
“Her,” said Will, quite willing to provoke the charming Mrs. Lydgate. “With a perfect woman, you don't think about separate qualities. You simply feel her presence.”
“I shall be jealous whenever Tertius visits Lowick,” Rosamond said with airy playfulness, her dimples showing. “He'll come home and think nothing of me.”
“It doesn't seem to have affected Lydgate that way so far. Mrs. Casaubon is too different from other women for comparisons.”
“I see you're a devoted worshipper. I suppose you see her often.”
“No,” said Will, almost petulantly. “Worship is generally more theoretical than practical. But I'm practising it to excess at this very moment. I really must tear myself away.”
“Do come back some evening. Mr. Lydgate would enjoy hearing the music, and I can't enjoy it quite as much without him.”

When her husband returned, Rosamond stood facing him, holding his coat collar in both hands. “Mr. Ladislaw was here singing with me when Mrs. Casaubon called,” she said. “He seemed annoyed. Do you think he disliked her finding him at our house? Surely your social position is at least as good as his, whatever his connection with the Casaubons.”
“No, no. If he really was annoyed, there must have been another reason. Ladislaw's something of a gypsy. He doesn't care about outward distinctions.”
“Apart from the music, he isn't always very pleasant. Do you like him?”
“Yes, I think he's a good fellow. A bit of a collection of odds and ends, but likeable.”
“You know, I think he worships Mrs. Casaubon.”
“Poor devil!” said Lydgate, smiling as he pinched his wife's ears.

Rosamond was beginning to feel she knew a great deal about the world. In particular, she had discovered something she could scarcely have imagined as an unmarried girl except as a vague tragedy played out in old-fashioned clothes: even married women could make conquests and enslave men. Country girls at that time, including those educated at Mrs. Lemon's, read little French literature more recent than Racine. Newspapers had not yet thrown their present magnificent light on life's scandals. Still, vanity, with a woman's whole mind and day at its disposal, can build abundantly on the smallest suggestions—especially the suggestion of limitless conquests. How delightful to take prisoners from the throne of marriage, a husband beside you as crown prince, though actually a subject himself! The captives would gaze up in perpetual hopelessness, probably losing their sleep, and if their appetites suffered too, so much the better. For the moment, however, Rosamond's romance centred chiefly on her crown prince. His certain submission was pleasure enough. When he said, “Poor devil!” she asked with playful curiosity:
“Why do you say that?”
“Well, what can a man do once he starts worshipping one of you mermaids? He just neglects his work and piles up debts.”

“You certainly don't neglect your work. You're always at the Hospital, visiting poor patients, or thinking about some medical quarrel. And at home you always want to study your microscope and little bottles. Admit it—you prefer them to me.”

“Aren't you ambitious enough to want your husband to become something more than a Middlemarch doctor?” Lydgate asked. He rested his hands on her shoulders and looked at her with affectionate seriousness. “I'll make you learn my favourite lines from an old poet:

‘Why should our pride make such a fuss to live
And be forgotten? What good equals this:
To do what merits writing, and to write
What merits reading and delights the world?’
That's what I want, Rosy: to do something worth writing about, and then write the account of it myself. A man has to work for that, my darling.”

“Of course I want you to make discoveries. Nobody could want more than I do for you to rise to an important position somewhere better than Middlemarch. You can't say I've ever tried to stop your work. But we can't live like hermits. You're not dissatisfied with me, are you, Tertius?”
“No, my dear. I'm altogether too content.”
“But what did Mrs. Casaubon come to ask you?”
“Only about her husband's health. But I think she's going to be wonderfully generous to our New Hospital. I believe she'll give us two hundred a year.”

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLIV
paragraphs:
I would not hug the coast, but sail
Into the open sea, steered by the stars.

Walking with Lydgate around the New Hospital's laurel-planted lawns, Dorothea learned that there was no sign of any change in Mr. Casaubon's physical condition. The only new symptom was mental: his anxiety to know the truth about his illness. She fell silent for a few moments, wondering whether something she had said or done had awakened that anxiety. Lydgate, unwilling to miss a chance to advance a cherished aim, ventured to speak.

“I don't know whether you or Mr. Casaubon have heard about the needs of our New Hospital. Circumstances have made it look rather self-serving for me to press the matter, though that isn't my fault. It's because the other medical men are fighting against it. I think these things generally interest you. I remember that when I first had the pleasure of meeting you at Tipton Grange, before your marriage, you asked me how the poor people's dreadful housing affected their health.”

“Yes, indeed,” said Dorothea, brightening. “I should be very grateful if you'd tell me how I could help improve things a little. All that sort of work has slipped away from me since I married. I mean,” she added after a brief hesitation, “the people in our village are reasonably comfortable, and I've been too preoccupied to look further. But here, in a place like Middlemarch, there must be so much that needs doing.”

“Everything needs doing,” Lydgate said with sudden energy. “This Hospital is an excellent undertaking. It owes its existence entirely to Mr. Bulstrode's efforts and largely to his money. But one man can't do everything in a project like this. Naturally he expected help. Instead, certain people in the town have stirred up a mean little feud against it, hoping to make it fail.”
“Why would they do that?” Dorothea asked in innocent astonishment.

“Mr. Bulstrode's unpopularity is the main reason to begin with. Half the town would almost go out of its way to frustrate him. In this foolish world, most people never think something worth doing unless their own circle does it. I had no connection with Bulstrode before coming here. I can view him impartially, and I see ideas and projects of his that I can turn to public benefit. If a reasonable number of better-educated men worked in the belief that their observations could help improve medical theory and practice, we'd soon see progress. That's how I look at it. To refuse to work with Mr. Bulstrode, I believe, would be to turn away from a chance to make my profession more useful to everyone.”
“I entirely agree,” said Dorothea, immediately absorbed by the situation he described. “But what do people have against Mr. Bulstrode? My uncle is friendly with him.”
“They dislike his religious manner,” Lydgate said, stopping there.
“Then there's all the more reason to despise their opposition,” said Dorothea, viewing Middlemarch affairs in the light of the great religious persecutions.

“To be fair, they have other objections. He's domineering and not very sociable. He's also involved in business, and business people have grievances of their own which I know nothing about. But what has that to do with whether it would be worthwhile to establish a hospital here more useful than any other in the county? The immediate reason for their opposition, though, is that Bulstrode has made me responsible for the medical management. Naturally I'm glad. It offers me a chance to do good work, and I know I have to justify his choice. As a result, however, the whole Middlemarch medical profession is fighting the Hospital tooth and nail. They won't cooperate themselves, and they try to discredit the entire enterprise and prevent donations.”
“How small-minded!” Dorothea exclaimed indignantly.

“I suppose you have to expect to fight your way forward. Hardly anything can be achieved without it. And the ignorance around here is astonishing. I claim nothing except that I've used opportunities not everyone has had. But there's no overcoming the offence of being young, newly arrived, and happening to know more than the established residents. Still, if I believe I can introduce better treatment, if I believe I can pursue observations and investigations that may benefit medicine permanently, I'd be a contemptible coward to let personal comfort stop me. And my course is clearer because no salary is involved to cast doubt on my motives for persisting.”

“I'm glad you've told me, Mr. Lydgate,” Dorothea said warmly. “I'm sure I can do a little to help. I have money and don't know what to do with it; that often troubles me. I can certainly spare two hundred a year for such a splendid purpose. How happy you must be, knowing things you're sure will do great good! I wish I could wake every morning with that knowledge. So much effort seems to go into things whose benefit one can hardly see.”
Her voice grew melancholy as she finished. Then, more cheerfully, she added, “Please come to Lowick and tell us more. I'll speak to Mr. Casaubon about it. I must hurry home now.”

She did speak of it that evening, saying she would like to contribute two hundred a year. Seven hundred a year, representing her own fortune, had been settled on her at marriage. Mr. Casaubon objected only with a passing remark that the amount might be disproportionate compared with the claims of other worthy causes. When Dorothea, in her ignorance, resisted the suggestion, he agreed. He did not care about spending money on himself and was willing to give it away. If a question of money ever stirred him deeply, it did so through some passion other than a love of material possessions.

Dorothea told him she had seen Lydgate and repeated the substance of their conversation about the Hospital. Mr. Casaubon asked no further questions, but was certain she had wanted to discover what had passed between the doctor and himself. “She knows that I know,” said the restless inner voice. Yet this additional unspoken knowledge only pushed confidence between them farther away. He distrusted her affection. And what loneliness can be lonelier than distrust?

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLV
paragraphs: Many people like to praise their ancestors' days and denounce the wickedness of their own. Yet they cannot do it well without borrowing the help and satire of the past. They condemn present vices in words describing the vices of the very times they praise, which surely proves that both ages share them. Horace, Juvenal and Persius were therefore no prophets, though their lines seem to indicate and point directly at our own times.—SIR THOMAS BROWNE: _Pseudodoxia Epidemica_.

Like other forms of opposition, the hostility to the New Fever Hospital which Lydgate had described to Dorothea could be viewed in many ways. To him it was a mixture of jealousy and thick-headed prejudice. Mr. Bulstrode saw professional jealousy too, but also a determination to frustrate him personally, prompted chiefly by hatred of the living religion he had tried to represent effectively as a layman. Certainly that hatred found excuses outside religion, excuses only too easily discovered in the tangled workings of human conduct. These might be called the administration's views. An opposition, however, has an unlimited supply of objections. It need never stop at the boundary of knowledge, but can draw endlessly on the vast territories of ignorance. Much of what Middlemarch said about the New Hospital and its management was certainly an echo, for heaven has taken care not to make everyone an original thinker. Yet there were differences reflecting every shade of society, from Dr. Minchin's polished restraint to the cutting declarations of Mrs. Dollop, landlady of the Tankard in Slaughter Lane.

The more Mrs. Dollop repeated her assertion, the more firmly she believed it: Dr. Lydgate meant to let patients die in the Hospital, if he didn't actually poison them, so that he could cut them up without asking anyone's permission. It was a known “fact” that he had wanted to cut up Mrs. Goby, as respectable a woman as any in Parley Street, who had money held in trust before she married. A poor story for a doctor! If he was any good, he ought to know what was wrong with you before you died, instead of poking about inside you afterwards. If that wasn't reason, Mrs. Dollop wanted to know what was. Her listeners generally felt her opinion was a defence: if it fell, there would be no end to cutting up bodies. Burke and Hare, with their pitch plasters, had shown that clearly enough. Middlemarch wanted none of that sort of business that ended on the gallows!

Do not suppose the opinions expressed at the Tankard in Slaughter Lane were unimportant to the medical profession. That venerable, genuine public house—the original Tankard, known as Dollop's—was the meeting place of a large mutual-benefit club. Some months earlier its members had voted on whether to dismiss their long-serving doctor, “Doctor Gambit,” in favour of “this Doctor Lydgate,” who could apparently perform astonishing cures and rescue people other practitioners had abandoned. Two members had tipped the vote against Lydgate. For private reasons they felt that the ability to revive people as good as dead was a doubtful recommendation, and might interfere with the favours of Providence. During the year, however, public feeling had changed, as the agreement at Dollop's now showed.

Well over a year earlier, before anyone knew anything about Lydgate's skill, judgments of it had naturally differed. They rested on a sense of probability located perhaps in the stomach or pineal gland. Though its verdicts varied, it remained a valuable guide where evidence was entirely absent. Patients with chronic illnesses, or lives worn thin like old Featherstone's, had immediately wanted to try him. Many people who disliked paying medical bills also welcomed the thought of opening an account with a new doctor. They could send for him freely whenever the children's temper needed a dose, occasions on which the established practitioners often became grumpy. Everyone inclined to employ Lydgate considered him likely to be clever. Some thought he might be better than the others “where the liver was concerned.” At least a few bottles of his “stuff” could do no harm. If they proved useless, one could return to the Purifying Pills, which kept you alive even if they failed to remove the yellowness. But these were relatively unimportant people. Respectable Middlemarch families would naturally not change doctors without a demonstrated reason. Nor did everyone who had employed Mr. Peacock feel obliged to accept a stranger simply because he was Peacock's successor. They objected that he was “unlikely to be as good as Peacock.”

Before long, however, enough details about Lydgate had circulated to produce more specific expectations and turn differences of opinion into partisanship. Some were those impressive facts whose significance is entirely concealed, like a statistical total without any standard of comparison but with an exclamation mark after it. Think what shudders the cubic feet of oxygen swallowed yearly by an adult man might have caused in certain Middlemarch circles! “Oxygen! Nobody knows what that is. Is it any wonder cholera has reached Dantzic? And yet some people claim quarantine does no good!”

One early rumour was that Lydgate did not dispense medicines. This offended both the physicians, whose exclusive distinction seemed threatened, and the surgeon-apothecaries, among whom he counted himself. Only a short time earlier, they might have expected the law to support them against a man who, without claiming a London M.D., dared to charge for anything except drugs. But Lydgate lacked the experience to foresee that his new practice would offend the public even more. Mr. Mawmsey, an important grocer in the Top Market, was not his patient, but questioned him pleasantly about it. Lydgate unwisely gave a quick explanation for the ordinary listener. He pointed out that if practitioners could earn their living only by presenting long bills for draughts, pills and mixtures, their professional character must suffer and the public would be continually harmed.

“That's how hardworking doctors can become almost as harmful as quacks,” Lydgate said rather carelessly. “To earn their bread, they have to overdose the king's subjects. That's a bad kind of treason, Mr. Mawmsey: fatally undermining the constitution.”

Mr. Mawmsey was an overseer of the poor, and his interview with Lydgate concerned relief paid outside the workhouse. He also had asthma and a growing family. He was therefore important medically as well as in his own estimation. Indeed, he was an exceptional grocer, with hair arranged in a flame-shaped pyramid and a shopkeeper's deference of the warm, encouraging kind. His compliments were jocular; he considerately refrained from unleashing the full force of his intellect. His friendly joking questions had set the tone of Lydgate's answer. But let the wise beware of explaining too readily. It multiplies the opportunities for error, lengthening a sum for people certain to miscalculate.

As Lydgate finished, he smiled and put his foot in the stirrup. Mr. Mawmsey laughed more than he would have if he had understood the doctor's reference to the king's subjects, and repeated, “Good morning, sir, good morning,” with the air of someone who saw the whole matter clearly. In fact, he was disturbed. For years he had paid precisely itemised bills, certain that every half-crown and eighteenpence represented something measurable delivered to him. He had done so contentedly as part of his duties as husband and father, seeing an unusually long bill as a distinction worth mentioning. Besides the substantial benefit the medicines brought to “self and family,” he enjoyed making shrewd assessments of their immediate effects and reporting intelligently to guide Mr. Gambit. This practitioner stood just below Wrench or Toller and was especially valued for attending childbirth. Mr. Mawmsey thought very little of his abilities in any other field, but in doctoring, he liked to say confidentially, he put Gambit above them all.

These were weightier reasons than a newcomer's superficial talk. That talk seemed flimsier still when repeated in the drawing room above the shop to Mrs. Mawmsey. A prolific mother, she was accustomed to being fussed over. Mr. Gambit attended her more or less frequently, and occasional attacks required Dr. Minchin.

“Does this Mr. Lydgate mean that taking medicine does no good?” asked Mrs. Mawmsey, who tended to drawl. “I'd like him to explain how I could get through Fair time without taking strengthening medicine for a month beforehand. Think what I have to provide for customers who call, my dear!” She turned to a close woman friend sitting nearby. “A big veal pie, a stuffed fillet, a round of beef, ham, tongue, and so on and so on! But it's the pink mixture that keeps me going best, not the brown. Mr. Mawmsey, I'm surprised that someone with _your_ experience could bear to listen. I'd have told him straight away that I knew better.”

“No, no, no,” Mr. Mawmsey replied. “I wasn't going to give him my opinion. My motto is: hear everything and judge for yourself. But he didn't know whom he was talking to. _He_ wasn't going to twist me around his finger. People often offer to teach me things when they might as well say, ‘Mawmsey, you're a fool.’ I simply smile. I humour everyone's little weakness. If medicine had harmed self and family, I'd have discovered it by now.”
The following day, Mr. Gambit heard that Lydgate was going about saying medicine was useless.
“Really!” he said, raising his eyebrows in guarded surprise. He was a stout, rough-voiced man with a large ring on his fourth finger. “Then how does he intend to cure his patients?”

“That's exactly what I say,” answered Mrs. Mawmsey, who habitually added force to her remarks by leaning heavily on the pronouns. “Does _he_ imagine people will pay just for him to sit with them and then leave?”

Mr. Gambit had spent a great deal of time sitting with Mrs. Mawmsey, giving detailed accounts of his own bodily habits and other concerns. Naturally he knew she intended no insinuation, since he had never charged for his spare time or personal stories. He answered jokingly:
“Well, you know, Lydgate is a handsome young man.”
“_I_ certainly wouldn't employ him,” said Mrs. Mawmsey. “_Other people_ can do as they like.”

Mr. Gambit could thus leave the leading grocer's house without fearing competition. He did, however, feel that Lydgate belonged to that class of hypocrites who advertise their own honesty to discredit other people. It might be worth someone's while to expose him. Yet Gambit's practice was satisfactory, rich in the smells of retail businesses which suggested that payments could be settled by balancing accounts. He thought it not worth exposing Lydgate until he knew how. His education was limited, and he had worked his way up against considerable professional contempt. But pronouncing the breathing organs “longs” made him no worse at delivering babies.

Other doctors felt better equipped. Mr. Toller shared the town's best practice and belonged to an old Middlemarch family. There were Tollers in law and every other occupation above retail trade. Unlike our irritable friend Wrench, he took apparent provocations with perfect ease. He was a well-bred man of quiet humour, kept a comfortable house, enjoyed a little sport when he could, was close to Mr. Hawley and hostile to Mr. Bulstrode. It may seem strange that someone with such pleasant habits should favour heroic treatment: bleeding, blistering and starving his patients with an impartial disregard for his own example. Yet the contrast enhanced his patients' opinion of his ability. They often remarked that his manner might be lazy, but his treatment was as vigorous as anyone could wish. Nobody took his profession more seriously, they said. He might be slow to arrive, but once he came, he _did_ something. He was much liked in his circle, and his casual irony gave twice the force to anything he implied against another person.

Naturally he tired of smiling and saying “Ah!” whenever he heard that Mr. Peacock's successor did not intend to dispense medicines. When Mr. Hackbutt mentioned it over the wine at a dinner party, Toller laughed and said, “Then Dibbitts will clear out his stale drugs. I like little Dibbitts. I'm pleased he's in luck.”

“I take your point, Toller,” said Mr. Hackbutt, “and entirely agree. I shall find an opportunity to say so. A doctor should answer for the quality of the medicines his patients consume. That is the reasoning behind the established system of charging. Nothing is more objectionable than parading reform when there is no actual improvement.”

“Parading it, Hackbutt?” Toller asked ironically. “I don't see how. A man can hardly parade something nobody believes in. There's no reform involved. The question is whether the doctor gets his profit on medicines from the chemist or from the patient, and whether there's an additional fee called attendance.”
“Exactly. Another damned new version of the old humbug,” said Mr. Hawley, handing the decanter to Mr. Wrench.
Usually restrained in his drinking, Mr. Wrench often took wine rather freely at parties and became more irritable as a result.

“‘Humbug’ is easy enough to throw around, Hawley,” he said. “What I object to is doctors fouling their own nest, raising an outcry across the country as if a general practitioner who dispenses medicine couldn't be a gentleman. I reject that accusation with contempt. The most ungentlemanly trick a man can play is to enter his profession with innovations that slander his colleagues' time-honoured methods. That's my opinion, and I'm prepared to defend it against anyone who disagrees.” Mr. Wrench's voice had grown extremely sharp.
“I can't oblige you by disagreeing, Wrench,” said Mr. Hawley, pushing his hands into his trouser pockets.

“My dear fellow,” Mr. Toller interposed soothingly, looking at Wrench, “the physicians have had their toes trodden on more than we have. If it's a matter of dignity, Minchin and Sprague are the ones to ask.”
“Does medical law offer no remedy against these encroachments?” Mr. Hackbutt asked, generously wishing to contribute his expertise. “What's the legal position, Hawley?”
“Nothing to be done legally,” Hawley replied. “I examined it for Sprague. You'd only smash your nose against some damned judge's ruling.”
“Nonsense, no need for law,” said Toller. “In practical terms, the attempt is ridiculous. Patients won't like it—certainly not Peacock's, who've been accustomed to being drained. Pass the wine.”

Toller's prediction proved partly correct. If the Mawmseys, who had no intention of employing Lydgate, were troubled by his supposed attack on medicine, his patients would inevitably watch with some anxiety to see whether he used every available means of treatment. Even kind Mr. Powderell, whose consistently charitable interpretations inclined him to respect Lydgate's apparent conscientious search for a better method, became doubtful during his wife's attack of erysipelas. He could not help mentioning that on a similar occasion Mr. Peacock had prescribed a series of pills. He could describe them only by their remarkable success in restoring Mrs. Powderell before Michaelmas from an illness that had begun in an unusually hot August. Finally, torn between not wanting to hurt Lydgate and fearing the omission of any “means,” he persuaded his wife secretly to take Widgeon's Purifying Pills. This respected Middlemarch remedy supposedly checked every disease at its source by acting immediately on the blood. They were not to tell Lydgate about this additional treatment. Mr. Powderell himself had no firm confidence in it, only a hope that it might carry a blessing.

At this uncertain stage of his arrival, however, Lydgate benefited from what we mortals rashly call good fortune. I suppose no new doctor ever settled anywhere without surprising someone with a cure. Such cures are fortune's testimonials, deserving as much credit as written or printed ones. Various patients recovered under Lydgate's care, some from dangerous illnesses. People remarked that the new doctor and his new methods at least had the merit of bringing patients back from death's door. The nonsense spoken on these occasions irritated Lydgate all the more because it gave him exactly the prestige an incompetent, unscrupulous man would want. The other doctors, simmering with dislike, would surely take it as evidence that he encouraged ignorant publicity. But even his proud frankness was restrained by the recognition that fighting ignorant interpretations was as useless as whipping fog. And “good fortune” insisted on employing them.

Mrs. Larcher had just begun taking a charitable interest in her cleaning woman's alarming symptoms when Dr. Minchin called. She asked him to examine the woman immediately and provide a certificate for the Infirmary. After examining her, he described the case in writing as a tumour and recommended that the bearer, Nancy Nash, be treated as an outpatient. On her way there, Nancy stopped at home and let the corset maker and his wife, whose attic she rented, read the doctor's paper. She consequently became a subject of sympathetic discussion in the neighbouring shops of Churchyard Lane. At first the tumour was said to be as large and hard as a duck's egg; later that day it had grown to the size of “your fist.” Most listeners agreed it would have to be cut out. But one knew oil, and another “squitchineal,” to be capable of softening and reducing any internal lump if enough was swallowed: oil by gradually making it supple, squitchineal by eating it away.

Meanwhile, Nancy reached the Infirmary on one of Lydgate's days there. After questioning and examining her, he told the resident surgeon quietly, “It isn't a tumour. It's cramp.” He prescribed a blistering treatment and an iron mixture and told her to rest at home. He also gave her a note for Mrs. Larcher, whom Nancy called her best employer, confirming that she needed nourishing food.

Before long Nancy became alarmingly worse in her attic. The supposed tumour had indeed yielded to the blister, but only by moving elsewhere and causing fiercer pain. The corset maker's wife fetched Lydgate. He visited Nancy at home for a fortnight, until his treatment restored her completely and she returned to work. Yet Churchyard Lane and other streets still called it a tumour, as did Mrs. Larcher herself. When Lydgate's remarkable cure was mentioned to Dr. Minchin, he naturally disliked saying, “It wasn't a tumour; I was wrong to call it that.” Instead he replied, “Really! Ah, I recognised a surgical case, not a fatal one.” Privately, however, he had been annoyed when he asked at the Infirmary about the woman he had referred two days earlier. The resident surgeon, a young man pleased to irritate Minchin without consequences, had told him exactly what happened. Minchin privately judged it improper for a general practitioner to contradict a physician's diagnosis so openly. Later he agreed with Wrench that Lydgate showed an unpleasant disregard for professional etiquette. Lydgate did not use the episode as a reason to admire himself or especially despise Minchin: equally qualified men often corrected one another's errors. But gossip took up this astonishing tumour, scarcely distinguished from cancer and considered more dreadful because it wandered. The proof of Lydgate's marvellous skill overcame much prejudice against his approach to medicines. Had he not rapidly restored Nancy Nash after she had rolled and rolled in agony from a hard, stubborn tumour that had nevertheless been forced to yield?

What could Lydgate do? When a lady is expressing amazement at your skill, telling her she is entirely mistaken and rather foolish is offensive. Explaining the nature of diseases would only add to his breaches of medical decorum. So he had to wince at the prospect of success founded on ignorant praise that overlooked every genuine merit.

With a more prominent patient, Mr. Borthrop Trumbull, Lydgate knew he had proved himself better than an ordinary doctor, though here too his advantage was doubtful. The eloquent auctioneer developed pneumonia. As a former patient of Mr. Peacock, he sent for Lydgate, whom he had already announced he intended to patronise. Mr. Trumbull was robust and therefore a good subject for the expectant method: observing the progress of an interesting illness while leaving it as far as possible to itself, recording its stages for future guidance. From the way he described his sensations, Lydgate guessed he would like to share his doctor's confidence and regard himself as a partner in the cure. Without much surprise, the auctioneer learned that his constitution, carefully watched, could be left to its own resources. It would offer a beautiful example of the disease with every phase clearly displayed. He probably possessed the rare mental strength to submit willingly to a trial of rational treatment, making the disorder of his lungs a benefit to society at large.
Mr. Trumbull agreed immediately, warmly adopting the view that an illness of his offered medical science no ordinary opportunity.

“Have no fear, sir. You're not addressing someone entirely ignorant of the _vis medicatrix_,” he said. His usual elevated manner sounded rather pathetic through his difficulty in breathing. He faced the absence of medicine without flinching. He was greatly supported by the thermometer's use, which implied the importance of his temperature; by knowing that he supplied specimens for the microscope; and by learning new words worthy of the dignity of his secretions. Lydgate was perceptive enough to indulge him in a little technical conversation.

It is easy to imagine Mr. Trumbull getting out of bed eager to discuss an illness that had demonstrated the strength of his mind as well as his body. Nor was he slow to praise the doctor who had recognised the quality of his patient. The auctioneer was not ungenerous. He enjoyed giving others their due, feeling he could afford it. He had picked up “expectant method” and rang changes on this and other learned phrases while declaring that Lydgate “knew a thing or two more than the other doctors—was far more deeply acquainted with the secrets of his profession than most of his colleagues.”

All this preceded Fred Vincy's illness, which gave Wrench's hostility a more definite personal basis. The newcomer already threatened to become an annoying rival. He was certainly annoying as a practical criticism of older, hard-pressed doctors who had had other things to do than concern themselves with untested ideas. His practice had expanded in a few directions. From the beginning, reports of his distinguished family had brought invitations everywhere, obliging the other doctors to meet him at dinner in the best houses. Being forced into company with someone you dislike does not invariably produce mutual affection. Rarely had they agreed so completely as in calling Lydgate arrogant, yet ready to crawl before Bulstrode in hopes of eventually dominating everyone himself. Mr. Farebrother, whose name was a leading banner for the anti-Bulstrode party, consistently defended and befriended him. This was attributed to Farebrother's inexplicable habit of fighting on both sides.

The ground was therefore thoroughly prepared for an outbreak of professional disgust when Bulstrode announced his rules for the New Hospital. They were especially infuriating because nobody could presently interfere with his wishes. Everyone except Lord Medlicote had refused to help finance the building, saying they preferred supporting the Old Infirmary. Bulstrode paid every expense. He had ceased regretting that he was buying the right to carry out his improvements without prejudiced colleagues obstructing him. But the sums were large and construction had dragged on. Caleb Garth had undertaken it, suffered business failure while it was in progress, and withdrawn from managing the business before the interior fittings began. Speaking of the Hospital, Caleb often said that whatever sort of metal Bulstrode might prove when tested, he liked sound carpentry and masonry and understood drains and chimneys. The Hospital had in fact become intensely important to Bulstrode. He would willingly have continued to pay a large annual sum to rule it without a board. But another cherished aim also needed money: he wanted to buy land near Middlemarch. He therefore hoped for substantial contributions to the Hospital's running costs. Meanwhile he drew up his system of management. The Hospital would treat fever in all its forms exclusively. Lydgate would be chief medical superintendent, free to conduct the comparative investigations whose importance his studies, especially in Paris, had revealed to him. Other visiting doctors could advise, but could not overrule his final decisions. General management would belong solely to five directors associated with Bulstrode, their voting strength proportional to their contributions. The board would fill its own vacancies. No crowd of small subscribers would have a share in governing it.
