Every doctor in the town immediately refused to serve as a visiting physician at the Fever Hospital.

“Very well,” Lydgate told Bulstrode. “Our resident surgeon and dispenser is excellent, clear-headed and skilful with his hands. We'll get Webbe from Crabsley to come twice a week. He's as good a country practitioner as any of them. Protheroe can come from Brassing for any unusual operation. I'll simply have to work harder. I've given up my post at the Infirmary. The project will succeed despite them, and then they'll be glad to join us. Things can't continue as they are. There'll soon have to be reforms of every kind, and then young men may be glad to study here.” He was in high spirits.

“You can rely on me not to draw back, Mr. Lydgate,” said Bulstrode. “As long as I see you vigorously pursuing high purposes, my support will be constant. I humbly trust that the blessing which has accompanied my efforts against this town's spirit of evil will continue. I have no doubt I can find suitable directors to assist me. Mr. Brooke of Tipton has already agreed and promised an annual contribution. He hasn't named the amount—probably it won't be large. But he will be a useful board member.”
A useful member might perhaps mean someone who would propose nothing and always vote with Mr. Bulstrode.

The doctors scarcely concealed their dislike of Lydgate now. Neither Dr. Sprague nor Dr. Minchin said they objected to his knowledge or desire to improve treatment. They objected to his arrogance, which nobody could wholly deny. They suggested that he was insolent and pretentious, addicted to the reckless innovation for noise and display that defined a charlatan.

Once the word “charlatan” was in circulation, nobody would let it drop. At that time the world was excited by Mr. St. John Long's miraculous performances. “Noblemen and gentlemen” testified that he had drawn a mercury-like fluid from a patient's temples.
One day Mr. Toller remarked to Mrs. Taft with a smile, “Bulstrode has found his match in Lydgate. A religious charlatan is bound to appreciate charlatans of other kinds.”

“Yes, indeed, I can well imagine,” Mrs. Taft replied, carefully keeping her count of thirty stitches in mind. “There are so many of them. I remember Mr. Cheshire and his irons, trying to straighten people whom the Almighty had made crooked.”

“No, no,” said Toller. “Cheshire was perfectly respectable, quite open and honest. St. John Long is the sort of man we call a charlatan: advertising cures by methods nobody understands, drawing attention to himself by pretending to penetrate deeper than other people. The other day he pretended to tap a man's brain and draw mercury from it.”
“Good heavens! What dreadful tampering with people's constitutions!” exclaimed Mrs. Taft.

After that, people in various quarters believed Lydgate experimented on even respectable constitutions for his own ends. How much more likely, then, that his irresponsible experiments would make a complete mess of hospital patients! Above all, as the Tankard's landlady had said, he could be expected to cut up their dead bodies without a thought. Lydgate had attended Mrs. Goby, who apparently died of a heart condition whose symptoms had been unclear. Too boldly, he had asked her relatives for permission to open the body. The offence spread quickly beyond Parley Street, where she had long lived on an income substantial enough to make any association of her body with Burke and Hare's victims a flagrant insult to her memory.

This was the state of affairs when Lydgate spoke to Dorothea about the Hospital. As we see, he met hostility and foolish misunderstanding with considerable spirit, knowing his own measure of success had helped provoke them.

“They won't drive me out,” he said in a confidential conversation in Mr. Farebrother's study. “I've got a good opportunity here to pursue what matters most to me, and I'm fairly sure I can earn enough for our needs. Before long I shall be working as quietly as possible. Nothing tempts me away from home and work now. And I'm increasingly convinced it will be possible to show that all tissues have the same origin. Raspail and others are following the same line, and I've been losing time.”
“I can't predict anything about that,” said Farebrother, who had been thoughtfully smoking his pipe as Lydgate spoke. “But you'll survive the town's hostility if you're careful.”

“What does being careful mean?” Lydgate asked. “I simply do the work in front of me. I can no more prevent people's ignorance and malice than Vesalius could. You can't adjust your behaviour to foolish conclusions nobody could foresee.”

“Quite right. That wasn't what I meant. I meant only two things. First, keep as independent of Bulstrode as possible. Naturally you can continue your own good work with his help, but don't become tied to him. Perhaps that sounds like personal feeling on my part, and I admit there's plenty of it. But personal feeling isn't always wrong when you reduce it to the impressions that make it simply an opinion.”

“Bulstrode means nothing to me except in public matters,” Lydgate replied casually. “I'm not fond enough of him to become closely attached. But what was your second point?” He was holding his leg in the most comfortable position and felt little need for advice.

“This: be careful—_experto crede_, trust someone who knows—not to get tangled up over money. Something you let slip one day told me you disapprove of how much I play cards for money. You're quite right. But try to avoid needing little sums you haven't got. Perhaps this advice is unnecessary. Still, a man likes to pretend he's risen above himself by displaying his own bad example and preaching about it.”

Lydgate received these hints warmly, though he would hardly have tolerated them from anyone else. He could not help remembering his recent debts. But they had seemed unavoidable, and he now intended only to keep a modest household. The furniture he owed for would not need replacing, nor would his wine supply for a long time.

Many thoughts encouraged him then, and rightly. A man who knows he is devoted to worthy aims can endure petty hostility by remembering great workers who fought their way forward and suffered wounds. They hover in his mind like patron saints, giving invisible help. Back at home that evening after his conversation with Farebrother, Lydgate stretched his long legs on the sofa, leaned his head back, and clasped his hands behind it in his favourite thinking posture. Rosamond sat at the piano, playing tune after tune. All her husband knew about them—emotional elephant that he was—was that they suited his mood like musical sea breezes.

Something in Lydgate's appearance just then was very fine. Anyone might have felt encouraged to wager on his success. His dark eyes, mouth and forehead had the calm that comes from the fullness of contemplative thought: a mind no longer searching but seeing, and a gaze seemingly filled by what lies behind it.
After a while Rosamond left the piano and sat on a chair beside the sofa, facing her husband.
“Have you had enough music, my lord?” she asked, folding her hands before her with a little air of submission.

“Yes, darling, if you're tired,” Lydgate said gently. He turned his eyes towards her and let them rest there, but otherwise did not move. At that moment her presence perhaps added no more than a spoonful to a lake, and her feminine instinct was quick to detect it.
“What's occupying you so completely?” she asked, leaning forward until her face was nearer his.
He brought his hands down and rested them gently behind her shoulders.
“I'm thinking of a great man who, three hundred years ago, was about my age and had already opened a new era in anatomy.”
“I can't guess who,” Rosamond said, shaking her head. “We played guessing games about historical figures at Mrs. Lemon's, but never anatomists.”
“I'll tell you. He was called Vesalius. The only way he could learn anatomy so thoroughly was to steal bodies at night from graveyards and execution grounds.”
“Oh!” Disgust crossed Rosamond's pretty face. “I'm very glad you aren't Vesalius. Surely he could have found some less horrible way.”

“No, he couldn't,” said Lydgate, too absorbed to pay much attention to her response. “To obtain a complete skeleton, he had to steal a criminal's bleached bones from the gallows, bury them, then secretly carry them away bit by bit in the middle of the night.”

“I hope he isn't one of your great heroes,” Rosamond said, half joking and half anxious. “Otherwise you'll be getting up at night to visit St. Peter's churchyard. Remember how angry you said people were about Mrs. Goby. You have quite enough enemies already.”

“So did Vesalius, Rosy. No wonder Middlemarch's medical old fogies are jealous. Some of the greatest doctors alive attacked Vesalius furiously because they believed Galen, and he proved Galen wrong. They called him a liar and a poisonous monster. But the facts of the human body supported him, so he defeated them.”
“What became of him afterwards?” Rosamond asked, somewhat interested.

“He had plenty of fighting to do right to the end. At one point they angered him so much that he burned a large amount of his work. Then he was shipwrecked on his way from Jerusalem to take an important professorship at Padua. His death was rather miserable.”
After a brief silence, Rosamond said, “You know, Tertius, I often wish you weren't a doctor.”
“No, Rosy, don't say that,” said Lydgate, drawing her closer. “It's like saying you wish you'd married someone else.”
“Not at all. You're clever enough to do anything. You could easily have chosen something else. And all your cousins at Quallingham think your choice of profession puts you below them.”
“My cousins at Quallingham can go to the devil!” Lydgate exclaimed contemptuously. “It was just like their impertinence if they said anything of the kind to you.”
“Still, darling, I _don't_ think it's a pleasant profession,” said Rosamond. As we know, she could maintain an opinion with considerable quiet persistence.

“It's the noblest profession in the world, Rosamond,” Lydgate said seriously. “To say you love me without loving the doctor in me is like saying you enjoy eating a peach but dislike its flavour. Please don't say it again, darling. It hurts.”

“Very well, Doctor Solemn-face,” said Rosy, dimpling. “From now on I'll declare that I adore skeletons, body-snatchers, little bits in bottles, and quarrels with everyone that end in your dying miserably.”
“No, no, it isn't as bad as that,” said Lydgate. He abandoned his protest and resigned himself to caressing her.

Pues no podemos haber aquello que queremos, queramos aquello que
podremos.
Since we cannot have what we want, let us want what we can have.—_Spanish proverb_.

While Lydgate, securely married and in charge of the Hospital, saw himself battling Middlemarch for medical reform, the town was becoming increasingly aware of the national struggle for reform of another kind.

By the time Lord John Russell's measure came before the House of Commons, Middlemarch had acquired a new political energy. Party divisions were sharper, and another election might reveal a clear shift in the balance. Some already predicted an election, declaring that the present Parliament would never pass a Reform Bill. Will Ladislaw repeatedly used this argument to assure Mr. Brooke that he was fortunate not to have tested his strength at the polls yet.

“Things will grow and ripen as if this were a comet year,” Will said. “Now Reform is on the agenda, public feeling will soon be as hot as a comet. There'll probably be another election before long, and by then Middlemarch will have a few more ideas in its head. For now we need to concentrate on the ‘Pioneer’ and political meetings.”

“Exactly, Ladislaw. We'll transform opinion here,” said Mr. Brooke. “Only, I want to stay independent on Reform, you know. I don't want to go too far. I'd like to follow Wilberforce and Romilly—work for the emancipation of enslaved black people, reform the criminal law, that sort of thing. Of course I'd support Grey.”

“If you believe in the principle of Reform, you must be ready to accept what circumstances make possible,” said Will. “If everyone fights for his own little piece against everyone else, the whole cause will fall apart.”

“Yes, yes, I agree. I quite see it that way. That's the light I'd put it in. I'd support Grey, you know. But I don't want to upset the balance of the constitution, and I don't think Grey would either.”

“But that change is what the country wants,” Will answered. “Otherwise political unions and every movement that knows its own purpose would mean nothing. People want a House of Commons weighted towards representatives of interests other than those of the landowners' nominees. Fighting for anything less would be like asking for just a piece of an avalanche that's already thundering down.”
“Excellent, Ladislaw. That's how to put it. Write it down. We must start gathering documents about the country's mood, as well as the machine-breaking and general hardship.”
“As for documents,” said Will, “a two-inch card would hold enough. A few lines of figures establish the misery. A few more will show how fast the people's political determination is growing.”

“Good. Develop that a little, Ladislaw. There's an idea. Write it up for the ‘Pioneer.’ Give the figures and deduce the misery, you know, then the other figures and deduce—and so forth. You have a way with words. Burke, now—thinking of Burke makes me wish someone had a pocket borough to give you. You'd never get elected, you know. We shall always need talent in the House, whatever reforms we make. That avalanche and thunder really sounded a little like Burke. That's what I want: not ideas, you understand, but a way of expressing them.”
“Pocket boroughs would be wonderful,” Ladislaw replied, “if they were always in the right pocket, with a Burke always available.”

Will was pleased by the flattering comparison, even from Mr. Brooke. It strains human endurance to know you express yourself better than others and never have it noticed. When admiration for the right thing is scarce, even an accidental bray of applause at exactly the right moment gives encouragement. Will felt his literary refinements usually lay beyond Middlemarch's perception. Still, he was beginning to enjoy thoroughly the work he had first accepted with a languid “Why not?” He studied politics as passionately as he had once studied poetic metres or the medieval world. Undeniably, without his wish to be near Dorothea, and perhaps his lack of any other plan, he would not now have been thinking about the English people's needs or criticising English statesmanship. He would probably have wandered through Italy, sketching plans for several plays, trying prose and finding it too thin, trying verse and finding it too artificial. He would have begun copying details from old paintings, stopped because they were “no good,” and remarked that cultivating oneself was, after all, the main thing. Politically he would have felt warm, general sympathy for freedom and progress. Our sense of duty often has to wait for work that replaces dilettantism and makes us feel that the quality of what we do actually matters.

Ladislaw had now accepted his share of work, though it was not the vaguely supreme achievement he had once imagined alone deserved sustained effort. His nature responded warmly to subjects visibly connected with life and action, and his easily roused rebelliousness helped kindle public spirit. Despite Mr. Casaubon and his exclusion from Lowick, he was fairly happy. He was gaining much new knowledge in a vivid, practical way and making the ‘Pioneer’ famous as far away as Brassing. Never mind how small an area that was: the writing was no worse than much that travels to the ends of the earth.
Mr. Brooke could be irritating. But alternating between visits to the Grange and retreats to his Middlemarch lodgings varied Will's life and eased his impatience.

“Move the pieces a little,” he told himself, “and Brooke could be in the Cabinet while I served as Under-Secretary. That's the usual arrangement. Little waves form the large ones, following the same pattern. I'm better off here than in the life Casaubon would have trained me for, with every action fixed by precedents too rigid for me to influence. Prestige and high pay don't interest me.”

As Lydgate had observed, he was something of a gypsy, rather enjoying the feeling that he belonged to no class. His position seemed romantic to him. He liked knowing that he caused a little surprise wherever he went. That pleasure had been disturbed when, during their accidental meeting at Lydgate's, he sensed a new distance between himself and Dorothea. His anger turned towards Mr. Casaubon, who had predicted that Will would lose social standing. “I never had any standing,” he would have answered, had the prophecy reached him, colour coming and going like breath beneath his transparent skin. But enjoying defiance is one thing; enjoying its consequences is another.

Meanwhile, the town's opinion of the new editor of the ‘Pioneer’ increasingly supported Mr. Casaubon's view. Will's distinguished family connection did not give him the advantage of an introduction as Lydgate's had. If people said young Ladislaw was Mr. Casaubon's nephew or cousin, they also said that “Mr. Casaubon wouldn't have anything to do with him.”

“Brooke has taken him up,” said Mr. Hawley, “because it's exactly what no sane person would expect. You can be sure Casaubon has damned good reasons for turning his back on a young man whose upbringing he paid for. Typical Brooke: the sort of fellow who'd praise a cat when trying to sell a horse.”

Some of Will's more or less poetic peculiarities seemed to support Mr. Keck, editor of the ‘Trumpet,’ in asserting that Ladislaw was not only a Polish agent but, if the truth were known, mentally unbalanced. That explained his unnatural speed and fluency whenever he took the platform—which he did at every opportunity, speaking with an ease that reflected badly on solid Englishmen everywhere. Keck found it revolting to see a slender young fellow with light curls stand up and declaim for an hour against institutions “already in existence when he lay in his cradle.” In a ‘Trumpet’ editorial, Keck described his speech at a Reform meeting as “the violence of an energumen—a wretched attempt to use brilliant fireworks to conceal the audacity of irresponsible claims and the poverty of knowledge cheaply and recently acquired.”
“That was a lively article yesterday, Keck,” Dr. Sprague remarked sarcastically. “But what is an energumen?”
“Oh, an expression that came up during the French Revolution,” Keck replied.

This dangerous picture of Ladislaw contrasted strangely with other habits people noticed. He loved small children, partly for their looks and partly from affection. The smaller they were, provided their legs worked reasonably well, and the funnier their clothes, the more Will enjoyed surprising and delighting them. As we know, in Rome he liked wandering among poor people. He retained the taste in Middlemarch.

Somehow he had acquired a troop of comical children: little bareheaded boys in worn-out breeches, with scant shirt-tails hanging out; little girls tossing hair from their eyes to look at him; and brothers acting as guardians at the mature age of seven. He had led them on roaming expeditions to Halsell Wood in nutting season. After the cold weather began, he took them out one clear day to gather sticks for a bonfire in a hollow on the hillside. There he produced a small feast of gingerbread and improvised a Punch-and-Judy play with puppets he had made himself. That was one oddity. Another was his habit of lying at full length on the rug while talking in houses where he felt at home. Occasional visitors would discover him there, and such irregular behaviour tended to confirm their suspicions of his dangerously mixed ancestry and general lack of principle.

His articles and speeches, however, naturally recommended him to families whom the sharper party divisions had placed on the Reform side. He received invitations to Mr. Bulstrode's, though he could not lie on the rug there. Mrs. Bulstrode felt that the way he spoke of Catholic countries, as though there could be a truce with Antichrist, illustrated intellectual men's usual tendency towards unsound belief.

At Mr. Farebrother's, he became a favourite with the ladies. Events had ironically placed Farebrother on Bulstrode's side in national politics. Little Miss Noble was especially fond of Will. One of his odd habits was to offer his arm whenever he met her carrying her small basket in the street. In full view of the town, he would insist on escorting her on a visit to distribute the little treats she secretly saved from her own share of sweets.

But he visited Lydgate's most often, and spent most time on its rug. The two men were entirely different, which did nothing to prevent their getting on. Lydgate was abrupt but not touchy, and paid little attention to healthy people's whims. Ladislaw did not generally waste his sensitivities on those who ignored them. With Rosamond, however, he sulked, behaved capriciously, and was often uncomplimentary, much to her private surprise. Nevertheless, his help with her music, his varied conversation and his freedom from grave preoccupations were gradually making him essential to her amusement. Her husband's absorption in serious matters, despite all his tenderness and indulgence, often made his behaviour unsatisfying to her and strengthened her dislike of medicine.

Lydgate sometimes subjected Will to awkward questions. He was inclined to sarcasm about people's superstitious faith in “the Bill” while nobody cared about the poor state of pathology. One March evening, Rosamond sat at the tea table in a cherry-coloured dress trimmed at the throat with swansdown. Lydgate, recently home and tired from his rounds, sat sideways in an armchair by the fire, one leg over its arm. His brow looked troubled as his eyes wandered over the ‘Pioneer's’ columns. Rosamond noticed his agitation and avoided looking at him, inwardly thanking heaven that she was not moody herself. Will lay on the rug, gazing absently at the curtain pole and softly humming “When first I saw thy face.” The spaniel, also stretched out but with little choice of space, looked between its paws at the intruder on its rug with silent, emphatic disapproval.
As Rosamond brought his tea, Lydgate threw down the paper and addressed Will, who had jumped up and gone to the table.
“There's no point advertising Brooke as a reforming landlord, Ladislaw. It only makes the ‘Trumpet’ find more fault with him.”

“No matter. ‘Pioneer’ readers don't read the ‘Trumpet,’” said Will, swallowing his tea and pacing about. “Do you think the public reads in order to change its opinions? We'd have a witches' brew then, with a vengeance: ‘Mingle, mingle, mingle, mingle, you who can may mingle.’ Nobody would know which side to take.”
“Farebrother doesn't think Brooke would win if an election came. The very men claiming to support him would pull another candidate out of the bag at the right moment.”
“It can't hurt to try. It's good to have MPs who live in the constituency.”
“Why?” asked Lydgate, fond as he was of using that inconvenient word abruptly.

“They represent the local stupidity more faithfully,” Will said, laughing and shaking his curls. “And the neighbourhood keeps them on their best behaviour. Brooke isn't a bad fellow, but he's made improvements on his estate that he'd never have made without this parliamentary ambition.”
“He isn't suited to public life,” Lydgate declared contemptuously. “He'd disappoint everyone relying on him. I see it at the Hospital, though there Bulstrode holds the reins and drives him.”

“That depends on the standard you set for public men,” Will replied. “He's good enough for the present purpose. Once people have made up their minds, as they're doing now, they don't need a personality. They only need a vote.”
“That's typical of political writers, Ladislaw. You praise a measure as if it cured everything, and promote men who are part of the disease that needs curing.”
“Why not? Men can help cure themselves out of existence without realising it,” said Will, who could invent reasons on the spot for questions he had not considered before.

“That doesn't justify encouraging wildly exaggerated hopes for this particular measure. You help the demand to swallow it whole and send voting parrots to Parliament who can do nothing except pass it. You oppose corruption, but nothing is more thoroughly corrupt than persuading people that political hocus-pocus can cure society.”

“Very fine, my dear fellow. But your cure has to begin somewhere. Suppose a thousand things that degrade the population cannot be changed until this particular reform comes first. Consider what Stanley said the other day: the House has spent long enough tinkering with small cases of bribery, asking whether some voter received a guinea, when everyone knows seats are sold wholesale. Wait for wisdom and conscience in public officials? Nonsense! The only conscience we can rely on is an entire class's powerful sense of injustice. The most effective wisdom is the wisdom of balancing claims. That's my starting point: which side is being wronged? I support whoever advances its claims, rather than some virtuous defender of injustice.”
“Applying general statements to a particular case merely assumes what you have to prove, Ladislaw. Saying I favour the dose that cures doesn't mean I favour opium for a particular case of gout.”

“I'm not assuming the answer to our actual question: whether we should attempt nothing until we find spotless men to work with. Would you follow that rule? If one man would get a medical reform passed for you and another would oppose it, would you ask which had better motives, or even better brains?”

“Of course,” said Lydgate, recognising that he had been checkmated by a move he often used himself, “if we refused to work with the men available, everything would stop. Suppose the worst opinion of Bulstrode in this town were true. That wouldn't alter the fact that he has the intelligence and determination to do what I believe should be done in the matters I understand and care about most. But that's my sole reason for working with him,” he added rather proudly, remembering Farebrother's remarks. “Otherwise he means nothing to me. I wouldn't praise him for any personal reason. I'd avoid that.”

“Are you suggesting I praise Brooke for personal reasons?” Will asked, stung, turning sharply. For the first time he felt offended by Lydgate, perhaps all the more because he would have resisted any close investigation of how his relationship with Brooke had developed.

“Not at all,” said Lydgate. “I was only explaining my own conduct. A man can work towards a particular goal alongside people whose motives and general behaviour are questionable, provided he's certain of his own independence and knows he isn't pursuing private gain, either a position or money.”

“Then why not allow other people the same freedom?” Will demanded, still hurt. “My independence matters to me as much as yours does to you. You've no more reason to imagine I expect personal benefits from Brooke than I have to imagine you expect them from Bulstrode. Motives are matters of honour, I suppose. Nobody can prove them. As for money and worldly position,” he concluded, tossing back his head, “surely it's obvious that considerations like those don't govern me.”

“You've completely misunderstood me, Ladislaw,” Lydgate said in surprise. He had been so occupied with defending himself that he had not seen what Will might infer about his own situation. “Forgive me for unintentionally upsetting you. In fact, I'd be more inclined to accuse you of romantically disregarding your worldly interests. On politics, I meant only a bias in your thinking.”

“How unpleasant you're both being tonight!” Rosamond said. “I can't imagine why money had to enter into it. Politics and medicine are disagreeable enough to quarrel about. Those two subjects give you both plenty of opportunity to fight the whole world and each other.”
She looked mildly impartial as she spoke, getting up to ring the bell and then crossing to her worktable.
“Poor Rosy!” Lydgate said, extending a hand as she passed. “Cherubs don't enjoy arguments. Have some music. Ask Ladislaw to sing with you.”
After Will left, Rosamond asked her husband, “What made you so irritable this evening, Tertius?”
“Me? Ladislaw was the irritable one. He catches fire like tinder.”
“I mean earlier. Something had annoyed you before you came home. You looked cross, and that made you start arguing with Mr. Ladislaw. It hurts me when you look like that, Tertius.”
“Does it? Then I'm a brute,” Lydgate said, caressing her remorsefully.
“What had annoyed you?”
“Oh, things outside the house. Business.” In fact, it was a letter demanding payment of a furniture bill. But Rosamond was expecting a baby, and he wanted to protect her from worry.

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLVII
paragraphs:
True love has never loved in vain,
For love most true is greatest gain.
No skill can make it: it must grow
Where kindly elements allow.
So, at heaven's chosen time and place,
A little wildflower lifts its face,
Root reaching down and eye raised high,
Its shape bestowed by earth and sky.

Will Ladislaw's little argument with Lydgate took place on a Saturday evening. Back in his rooms, he sat up half the night, freshly irritated, reconsidering everything he had already thought about settling in Middlemarch and attaching himself to Mr. Brooke. His earlier doubts about taking that step had become a sensitivity to any suggestion that he should not have taken it. That explained his anger with Lydgate, an anger that still left him restless. Was he making a fool of himself, just when he felt more certain than ever that he was better than a fool? And for what purpose?

Well, for no definite purpose. He did have dreamy visions of possibilities. Nobody who possesses both feelings and thoughts fails to think under the influence of those feelings, to see images rise that soothe passion with hope or sting it with fear. But this universal experience varies widely. Will was not one of those whose intelligence stayed on the main road. He followed byways where he found small pleasures of his own choosing, pleasures that gentlemen cantering along the highway might consider idiotic. The happiness he made for himself out of his feeling for Dorothea was one example. Strange as it may seem, Mr. Casaubon's ordinary, vulgar suspicion had no power to tempt or absorb him: the prospect that Dorothea might become a widow, and that her interest in him might lead her to accept him as a husband. He did not inhabit that imagined scene and follow it through as we all follow the alternative life that serves as our practical heaven. It was not simply that he refused thoughts open to an accusation of baseness, or that he already felt uneasy about having to defend himself against a charge of ingratitude. An underlying awareness of the many barriers besides her husband that separated him from Dorothea also turned his imagination away from speculating about Casaubon's fate. There were other reasons too. As we know, Will could not bear the idea of a flaw in his crystal. The calm freedom with which Dorothea looked at him and spoke both delighted and exasperated him. Thinking of her exactly as she was gave such exquisite pleasure that he could not wish for a change which would somehow change her. Do we not avoid a fine melody reduced to a street tune? Do we not recoil on learning that a rarity—perhaps a carving or engraving, which we have contemplated with even greater delight because of the trouble required to glimpse it—is actually quite common and available for everyday ownership? Our good depends on the quality and breadth of our feelings. Will cared little for life's supposedly solid goods and greatly for its subtler influences. To carry within him such a feeling for Dorothea was like inheriting a fortune. What others might call the futility of his passion gave his imagination further delight. He felt an impulse of generosity, and found in his own experience the higher love poetry that had charmed his fancy. Dorothea, he told himself, sat enthroned for ever in his soul. No other woman could rise higher than her footstool. Had he been able to describe her effect on him in immortal verse, he might have boasted, like old Drayton, that:

“Queens in years to come might gladly live
On scraps of praise too plentiful for her.”

But that achievement was uncertain. What else could he do for Dorothea? What value did his devotion have for her? He could not tell. He would not move beyond her reach. Among her friends he saw nobody to whom he could imagine her speaking with the same simple confidence she showed him. She had once said she would like him to stay. Stay he would, whatever fire-breathing dragons hissed around her.

That was always where his doubts ended. Yet he could contradict and rebel even against his own decision. Often, as on this particular night, some outward sign irritated him by showing that his public work under Brooke's leadership could never look as heroic as he wished. This irritation always joined another: despite sacrificing his dignity for Dorothea, he hardly ever saw her. Unable to dispute those unpleasant facts, he disputed his own strongest inclination instead and said, “I'm a fool.”

Nevertheless, because the whole inward debate revolved around Dorothea, it ended as before by sharpening his sense of what her presence would mean to him. Suddenly remembering that tomorrow was Sunday, he decided to go to Lowick Church and see her. He went to sleep with that intention. But while he dressed in the rational morning light, Objection spoke:
“That would practically defy Mr. Casaubon's ban on visiting Lowick. Dorothea will be displeased.”
“Nonsense!” Inclination replied. “It would be outrageous for him to stop me visiting a pretty country church on a spring morning. And Dorothea will be pleased.”
“Casaubon will know perfectly well that you've come either to irritate him or to see Dorothea.”

“I'm not going to irritate him. And why shouldn't I see Dorothea? Must he have everything to himself and be comfortable all the time? Let him suffer a little, like everyone else. I've always liked the quaint church and congregation. Besides, I know the Tuckers. I'll sit in their pew.”

Having silenced Objection by sheer unreason, Will walked towards Lowick as if bound for Paradise. He crossed Halsell Common and skirted the wood, where broad sunlight shone beneath budding branches, revealing the beauty of moss and lichen and new green growth pushing through the brown. Everything seemed aware it was Sunday and approved his churchgoing. Will found happiness easy when nothing crossed his wishes. By now the thought of annoying Mr. Casaubon had become rather amusing. It brought out his merry smile, as pleasant to watch as sunlight breaking over water, though its cause was not admirable. Most of us, however, readily decide that anyone blocking our path is hateful. We do not mind giving him a little of the disgust his personality creates in us. Will walked with a small book under his arm and a hand in each side pocket. He never read, but sang a little while imagining scenes inside the church and on leaving it. He was testing tunes for some words of his own, sometimes borrowing an existing melody, sometimes inventing one. The words were not exactly a hymn, but they certainly suited his Sunday experience:

“Oh me, oh me, how little food
My hungry love is given!
A touch, a ray beyond my reach,
A shadow that has vanished:

“A dream of breath that might be near,
A voice that echoes inward,
The thought that someone holds me dear,
The place where I was welcomed,

“The trembling of a fear dispelled,
A hurt that never happened—
Oh me, oh me, how little food
My hungry love is given!”

Sometimes he took off his hat and tossed his head back as he sang, showing his delicate throat. Then he looked like spring itself made flesh, its spirit filling the air: a radiant creature rich in uncertain promises.

The bells were still ringing when he reached Lowick. He entered the curate's pew before anyone else arrived. Yet after the congregation had assembled, he remained alone there. The pew faced the rector's at the entrance to the small chancel. Looking around at the country faces, Will had time to fear that Dorothea would not come. Year after year this congregation gathered between the whitewashed walls and dark old pews with scarcely more change than the branches of a tree, some breaking with age while others put out shoots. Mr. Rigg's frog-like face was an alien, inexplicable addition. Despite that disturbance in the natural order, the Waules and country Powderells still sat side by side in their pews. Brother Samuel's cheeks were as round and purple as ever. Three generations of respectable cottagers came as before, conscious of their duty towards their social superiors in general. The youngest children probably regarded Mr. Casaubon, in his black gown and highest pulpit, as the chief of all their betters and the most terrible to offend. Even in 1831 Lowick was peaceful, stirred no more by Reform than by the Sunday sermon's solemn course. The congregation remembered Will's earlier appearances and scarcely noticed him, except for the choir, who expected him to make himself heard in the singing.

At last Dorothea appeared against this quaint background. She walked up the short aisle wearing her white beaver-fur bonnet and grey cloak, the same ones she had worn in the Vatican. Since she faced the chancel as she entered, even her short-sighted eyes soon recognised Will. Outwardly she showed her feelings only by growing a little pale and giving him a solemn bow as she passed. To his surprise, he suddenly felt uneasy. After returning her bow, he dared not look at her again. Two minutes later Casaubon came out of the vestry and sat in the pew facing her, completing Will's paralysis. He could look nowhere but towards the choir in the little gallery above the vestry door. Perhaps Dorothea was distressed; he had made a dreadful mistake. Annoying Casaubon was no longer amusing. Casaubon probably had the advantage of watching him and seeing that he dared not turn his head. Why had he not imagined this? Yet he could hardly have expected to sit alone in that square pew without the Tuckers to relieve him. Apparently they had left Lowick altogether, for a new clergyman occupied the reading desk. Still, he now called himself stupid for failing to foresee that he could not possibly look towards Dorothea, and that she might even think his visit impertinent. There was no escaping his cage. He found the places in his book and studied it like a schoolmistress. Never had morning service seemed so endlessly long. He felt utterly ridiculous, miserable and ill-tempered. This was the reward for worshipping the sight of a woman! The parish clerk noticed with surprise that Mr. Ladislaw did not join in the tune of Hanover, and supposed he might have a cold.

Mr. Casaubon did not preach that morning. Will's situation remained unchanged until the blessing was pronounced and everyone rose. At Lowick, custom allowed “the betters” to leave first. Suddenly determined to break the spell over him, Will looked straight at Casaubon. But Casaubon's eyes were fixed on the pew-door latch. He opened it, let Dorothea pass and followed immediately without looking up. As she turned out of the pew, Will caught her eye. Again she bowed, this time looking agitated, as though holding back tears. He followed them outside, but they went straight towards the little gate from the churchyard into the shrubbery without turning round.
He could not follow them. All he could do was walk sadly home at midday along the road he had travelled so hopefully that morning. Both around him and within him, the light had entirely changed.

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLVIII
paragraphs:
The golden hours are surely growing grey;
They dance no longer, try in vain to run.
I see their white hair streaming on the wind,
Each haggard face turned slowly towards me,
Held in the circling clasp that never loosens,
Driven by storms.

Dorothea's distress as she left church came mainly from seeing that Mr. Casaubon was determined not to speak to his cousin. Will's appearance had only made their estrangement more obvious. She thought his coming perfectly excusable, even a kindly attempt at the reconciliation she had so often wished for. Probably he had imagined, as she had, that if they could meet naturally, they would shake hands and friendship might return. Now that hope seemed entirely lost. Will was more completely banished than ever, for being forced to see a man he refused to acknowledge must have renewed Mr. Casaubon's bitterness.

Her husband had felt unwell that morning, with some difficulty breathing, and had therefore not preached. She was unsurprised by his near silence at lunch, and still less by his failure to mention Will Ladislaw. As for herself, she felt she could never raise the subject again. On Sundays they usually spent the hours between lunch and dinner apart. Casaubon mostly dozed in the library, while Dorothea read favourite books in her sitting room. A little pile lay on the table in the bow window, ranging from Herodotus, which she was learning to read with her husband, to her old companion Pascal and Keble's ‘Christian Year.’ Today she opened them one after another and could read none. Everything was dreary: the omens before Cyrus's birth, Jewish antiquities—oh dear!—devotional sayings, the sacred music of favourite hymns. All sounded as flat as tunes tapped out on wood. Even the spring flowers and grass seemed to shiver dully beneath the afternoon clouds that intermittently hid the sun. Even her habitual sustaining thoughts carried the weariness of long future days in which they would remain her only companions. Poor Dorothea hungered for a different, fuller companionship. The endless effort of married life had increased that hunger. She was always trying to become what her husband wanted, never able to rest in his delight in what she already was. Whatever she liked, whatever she naturally wanted, always seemed excluded from her life. If her husband merely allowed it without sharing it, he might as well have forbidden it. They had disagreed about Will Ladislaw from the start. Since Casaubon's harsh rejection of her strong feelings about Will's claims on the family property, she had become convinced that she was right and her husband wrong, but that she could do nothing. That afternoon her helplessness numbed her more miserably than ever. She longed for people she could love and who could love her. She longed for work as directly beneficial as sunshine and rain. Instead, she seemed destined to live increasingly in a tomb, among the machinery of a ghastly labour producing something that would never see daylight. Today she had stood at the tomb's entrance and watched Will Ladislaw retreat into the distant world of warm activity and companionship, turning his face towards her as he went.

Books were useless. Thought was useless. It was Sunday, so she could not take the carriage to see Celia, who had recently had a baby. There was no escape from spiritual emptiness and discontent. Dorothea had to endure her low spirits as she would a headache.
After dinner, when she usually began reading aloud, Mr. Casaubon suggested going to the library. He had ordered a fire and lights there, he said. He seemed revived and deep in thought.
In the library, Dorothea noticed that he had rearranged a row of notebooks on a table. He picked up a familiar volume containing an index to all the others and put it in her hand.

“You would oblige me, my dear,” he said, sitting down, “if instead of our usual reading you went through this aloud tonight, pencil in hand. Whenever I say ‘mark,’ make a cross. This is the first stage of a process of selection I have long contemplated. As we proceed, I shall explain the principles governing the choices, so that you may, I hope, take an informed part in my purpose.”

Since his memorable conversation with Lydgate, there had been many signs that Casaubon's initial reluctance to let Dorothea work with him had given way to the opposite tendency: demanding considerable interest and labour from her. This proposal was another.

After two hours of reading and marking, he said, “We shall take the volume upstairs, and the pencil too, please. If we read during the night, we can continue. I trust this does not tire you, Dorothea?”
“I always prefer reading whatever you most want to hear,” she answered truthfully. What she dreaded was making an effort, in reading or anything else, that left him as joyless as before.

That certain qualities in Dorothea impressed themselves powerfully on others was proved by her husband's absolute trust in her promises and in her ability to devote herself to what she thought right and best, despite all his jealousy and suspicion. Lately he had begun to regard these qualities as his own special possession. He wanted to claim them entirely.

The night reading did take place. Young and exhausted, Dorothea fell asleep quickly and deeply. Light awakened her, seeming at first like a sudden view of sunset after climbing a steep hill. Opening her eyes, she saw her husband in his warm dressing gown settling into the armchair by the fireplace, where embers still glowed. He had lit two candles, expecting her to wake but reluctant to rouse her more directly.
“Are you unwell, Edward?” she asked, getting up at once.
“Lying down made me uncomfortable. I shall sit here a while.” She added wood to the fire, wrapped herself warmly, and asked, “Would you like me to read?”
“I should be most grateful, Dorothea,” Casaubon answered. There was a little more meekness than usual in his politeness. “I cannot sleep. My mind is extraordinarily clear.”
“I'm afraid the stimulation might be too much,” she said, remembering Lydgate's warnings.

“No, I feel no excessive excitement. Thinking comes easily.” She dared not insist. For an hour or more she read according to the evening's plan, but moved through the pages faster. Casaubon's mind was more alert. The slightest hint of wording seemed enough for him to anticipate what followed. “That will do—mark it,” he would say, or, “Go on to the next heading. I shall leave out the second digression on Crete.” Dorothea marvelled at his mind sweeping like a bird over ground it had crawled across for years. Finally he said:

“Close the book, my dear. We shall continue tomorrow. I have delayed too long and should be glad to finish. You see, however, the principle governing my choices: to supply sufficient illustration, without disproportion, for each thesis listed in the present draft of my introduction. You understand that clearly, Dorothea?”
“Yes,” she answered, her voice a little unsteady. Her heart felt sick.
“I think I can rest now,” said Casaubon. He lay down again and asked her to extinguish the candles. Once she too was in bed, with only a dull glow from the hearth breaking the darkness, he spoke.
“Before I sleep, Dorothea, I have something to ask.”
“What is it?” she said, inwardly afraid.
“I ask you to consider carefully and tell me whether, if I die, you will carry out my wishes. Will you refrain from doing what I should disapprove of, and devote yourself to what I should want?”
The request did not surprise her. Many recent incidents had made her suspect some intention in her husband that would place another burden on her. She did not answer at once.
“You refuse?” His voice grew sharper.

“No, I haven't refused,” Dorothea said clearly, her need for freedom asserting itself. “But it's too solemn a matter. I don't think it's right to promise without knowing what the promise will require. Whatever love asked of me, I would do without a promise.”
“But you would follow your own judgment. I ask you to follow mine. You refuse.”

“No, dear, no!” she pleaded, crushed between opposing fears. “But may I have a little time to think? With all my soul, I want to comfort you. But I can't give a pledge suddenly, especially without knowing what I'm pledging to do.”
“Then you cannot trust the nature of my wishes?”
“Give me until tomorrow,” she begged.
“Until tomorrow, then,” said Casaubon.

Soon she heard him sleeping, but sleep would not return to her. She forced herself to lie still so as not to disturb him, while a battle raged in her mind and imagination marshalled its forces first on one side, then the other. She had no suspicion that the control he wanted over her future might concern anything beyond his work. But she could see plainly that he would expect her to devote herself to sifting those mixed heaps of material, intended as doubtful illustrations of still more doubtful principles. The poor girl had completely lost faith in the reliability of the Key that had been her husband's lifelong ambition and labour. Despite her limited education, it was unsurprising that her judgment was sounder than his. She brought unprejudiced comparison and healthy common sense to possibilities on which he had staked his whole self-esteem. Now she imagined days, months and years sorting what might be called broken mummies and fragments of a tradition itself pieced together from crushed ruins. She would sort them to feed a theory already withered at birth, like a changeling. Certainly an energetic mistake pursued energetically can keep embryonic truths alive. The search for gold also investigates substances; the body of chemistry is prepared for its soul, and Lavoisier is born. But Casaubon's theory about the elements from which all tradition sprang was unlikely to stumble against any discoveries. It drifted among pliable guesses, no firmer than the derivations of words once thought convincing because they sounded alike, until that very likeness was shown to make the derivations impossible. His interpretive method never faced the test of creating anything that met harder resistance than an elaborate account of Gog and Magog. It could proceed as untroubled as a plan to string the stars together. And how often Dorothea had already suppressed weariness and impatience with this dubious riddle-solving, which had replaced the shared pursuit of high knowledge she thought would ennoble her life! Now she understood why her husband clung to her as perhaps his last hope of putting his work into publishable form. At first he had seemed determined to keep even her from knowing closely what he did. But gradually the terrible pressure of human need, the prospect of death coming too soon—

Here her pity turned from her own future to his past, and to his present struggle with the fate that past had created. The lonely labour, ambition barely breathing beneath self-doubt, the goal retreating as his limbs grew heavier—and now the sword visibly trembling overhead! Had she not wanted to marry him to help with his life's work? But she had believed it would be something greater, something she could serve devotedly for its own sake. Would it be right, even to ease his grief, to labour fruitlessly on a treadmill? Could she do it, even after promising?

Yet could she deny him? Could she say, “I won't satisfy this wasting hunger”? She would be refusing him after death what she would almost certainly do while he lived. If, as Lydgate had said was possible, he lived another fifteen years or more, her life would certainly be spent helping and obeying him.

Still, devotion to a living man differed profoundly from an undefined promise of devotion to the dead. While he lived, she would remain free to object to any demand and even refuse it. But might he intend to ask something beyond anything she had imagined, since he wanted a pledge without telling her exactly what he wished? The thought crossed her mind more than once, though she could not believe it. No: only his work held his heart. That was the purpose for which her life must extend his failing one.
And if she now said, “No! When you die, I won't lift a finger for your work,” it seemed she would crush his already wounded heart.

For four hours she lay struggling, until she felt ill and bewildered, unable to decide, praying silently. Helpless as a child who has sought and sobbed too long, she finally slept late into the morning. When she woke, Casaubon was already up. Tantripp said he had read prayers, eaten breakfast and gone to the library.
“I've never seen you so pale, madam,” said Tantripp, the solidly built woman who had been with the sisters in Lausanne.
“Was I ever rosy-cheeked, Tantripp?” Dorothea asked with a faint smile.

“Well, not exactly rosy, but you had a bloom like a China rose. Always breathing in those leather books—what can anyone expect? Rest a little this morning, madam. Let me say you're ill and can't come into that stuffy library.”
“Oh, no, no! I must hurry,” Dorothea said. “Mr. Casaubon particularly needs me.”
By the time she went downstairs, she felt certain she would promise to fulfil his wishes. But later in the day, not yet.
As she entered the library, Casaubon turned from the table where he had been arranging books.

“I was waiting for you, my dear. I hoped to begin work immediately this morning, but I feel somewhat unwell, probably from yesterday's excessive excitement. As the air is milder, I shall take a walk among the shrubs.”
“I'm glad of that,” said Dorothea. “I was afraid your mind was too active last night.”
“I should like it set at rest on the last matter we discussed. I hope you can give me your answer now.”
“May I join you in the garden shortly?” she asked, gaining a little breathing space.
“I shall be in the Yew-tree Walk for the next half hour,” he replied, and left her.

Exhausted, Dorothea rang for Tantripp to bring her outdoor things. She had sat still for a few minutes, but without renewing her inward struggle. She simply felt she was about to say yes to her own doom. Too weak and too afraid of inflicting a sharp wound on her husband, she could do nothing except submit completely. She remained seated while Tantripp put on her bonnet and shawl. Such passivity was unusual; she normally liked to dress herself.
“God bless you, madam!” Tantripp said. Having finished tying the bonnet, she felt an irresistible rush of love for the beautiful, gentle creature she could do no more to help.

That was too much for Dorothea's strained feelings. She burst into tears and sobbed against Tantripp's arm. Soon, though, she mastered herself, wiped her eyes, and went through the glass door into the shrubbery.

“I wish every book in that library was built into a cattycomb for your master,” Tantripp told Pratt, the butler, whom she found in the breakfast room. As we know, she had visited Rome and its antiquities. When speaking to the other servants she always refused to call Casaubon anything except “your master.”
Pratt laughed. He liked his master well enough, but liked Tantripp better.

Outside on the gravel paths, Dorothea paused among the nearest groups of trees, hesitating as she had once before, though for a different reason. Then she had feared her offer of companionship would be unwelcome. Now she dreaded the place where she knew she must bind herself to a companionship from which she recoiled. Neither law nor public opinion compelled her, only her husband's nature and her own compassion: the imagined bond of marriage, not its actual requirements. She understood the whole situation clearly, yet remained bound. She could not strike the wounded soul appealing to hers. If that was weakness, Dorothea was weak. But the half hour was passing; she must delay no longer. Entering the Yew-tree Walk, she could not see him. The path curved, however, and she went on expecting to find his figure in the blue cloak and warm velvet cap he wore in the garden on chilly days. Perhaps he was resting in the summerhouse, she thought, a little way off the path. Rounding the corner, she saw him on the bench beside a stone table. His arms rested on it and his forehead lay on his arms. His blue cloak had been pulled forward, hiding his face on either side.

“He exhausted himself last night,” she thought. At first she supposed he was asleep and that the summerhouse was too damp for resting. Then she remembered how lately he had adopted this position while she read, as though finding it more comfortable than any other. Sometimes he spoke, as well as listened, with his face lowered like that. She entered the summerhouse and said, “I've come, Edward. I'm ready.”

He gave no sign of hearing. Thinking he must be deeply asleep, she put her hand on his shoulder and repeated, “I'm ready.” Still he did not move. With a sudden, confused fear, she bent towards him, removed his velvet cap and pressed her cheek close to his head, crying in distress:
“Wake up, dear, wake up! Listen to me. I've come to give my answer.” But Dorothea never gave it.

Later that day, Lydgate sat beside her bed while she talked deliriously, thinking aloud and repeating what had passed through her mind the previous night. She recognised him and used his name, but seemed convinced she ought to explain everything to him. Again and again she begged him to explain it all to her husband.
“Tell him I'll come soon. I'm ready to promise. Only, thinking about it was so terrible that it made me ill. Not very ill. I'll soon recover. Go and tell him.”
But the silence in her husband's ears would never be broken again.

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLIX
paragraphs:
“A task too strong for wizard spells
This squire had brought about;
’T is easy dropping stones in wells,
But who shall get them out?”
“I wish to God we could keep Dorothea from hearing about this,” said Sir James Chettam. His brow was slightly furrowed, and his mouth showed profound disgust.
He stood on the hearthrug in the library of Lowick Grange, talking to Mr. Brooke. Mr. Casaubon had been buried the previous day, and Dorothea was still too ill to leave her room.

“That would be difficult, Chettam, you know. She's an executor, and she likes looking into these matters—property, land, things of that sort. She has ideas of her own, you know,” said Mr. Brooke. He nervously put on his eyeglasses and examined the edges of a folded paper in his hand. “And she'll want to take part—you may be sure that as an executor Dorothea will insist on taking part. Besides, she turned twenty-one last December, you know. I can't prevent anything.”

Sir James stared silently at the carpet for a moment. Then he suddenly raised his eyes and fixed them on Mr. Brooke. “I'll tell you what we can do. We must keep all business away from Dorothea until she recovers, and the moment she can be moved, she must come to us. Being with Celia and the baby will be the very best thing for her, and help her pass the time. Meanwhile, you must get rid of Ladislaw: you must send him out of the country.” At this, the full intensity of his disgust returned to Sir James's face.
Putting his hands behind his back, Mr. Brooke walked to the window and gave himself a little shake to straighten up before answering.
“Easily said, Chettam. That's easily said, you know.”
“My dear sir,” Sir James insisted, keeping his indignation within the bounds of respect, “you brought him here, and you're keeping him here—through the work you give him, I mean.”

“Yes, but I can't suddenly dismiss him without giving reasons, my dear Chettam. Ladislaw has been invaluable, entirely satisfactory. I believe I've done this district a service by bringing him—by bringing him, you know.” Mr. Brooke turned round to finish with a nod.

“Then it's a pity this district couldn't have managed without him. That's all I can say. In any event, as Dorothea's brother-in-law, I believe I'm entitled to object strongly to her friends doing anything that keeps him here. You must admit I have a right to speak when my wife's sister's dignity is at stake?”
Sir James was growing heated.
“Certainly, my dear Chettam, certainly. But your ideas and mine are different—different—”

“Not about this thing Casaubon has done, I hope,” Sir James broke in. “I say he has compromised Dorothea most unfairly. Nothing could be meaner or less worthy of a gentleman than this—adding such a codicil to a will he made when he married, a will her family knew of and relied on. It's a direct insult to Dorothea!”

“Well, Casaubon was rather unreasonable about Ladislaw, you know. Ladislaw explained the reason to me—disliked the direction he'd taken, you know. Ladislaw didn't think much of Casaubon's theories, Thoth and Dagon—all that. And I fancy Casaubon resented the independent position Ladislaw had established. I saw their letters to one another, you know. Poor Casaubon was rather buried in his books—he knew nothing of the world.”

“Ladislaw may choose to present it that way,” said Sir James. “But I believe Casaubon was simply jealous of him because of Dorothea. People will assume she gave him some cause, and that's what makes it so abominable—linking her name with this young fellow's.”

“My dear Chettam, nothing will come of it, you know,” said Mr. Brooke, sitting down and putting on his eyeglass again. “It's entirely in keeping with Casaubon's odd ways. Take this paper, ‘Synoptical Tabulation’ and so forth, ‘for the use of Mrs. Casaubon.’ It was locked in the desk with the will. Presumably he wanted Dorothea to publish his research, eh? And she'll do it, you know. She's taken an extraordinary interest in his studies.”
“My dear sir,” said Sir James impatiently, “that has nothing to do with it. The question is whether you agree that young Ladislaw ought to be sent away.”

“Well, no—I don't see the urgency. Perhaps it will work itself out in time. As for gossip, sending him away won't stop that, you know. People say whatever they want to say, whether they have evidence for it or not,” said Mr. Brooke, growing perceptive about truths that supported his own wishes. “I could get rid of Ladislaw up to a point—take the ‘Pioneer’ away from him, that sort of thing. But I couldn't force him out of the country if he didn't want to go—didn't want to, you know.”
Mr. Brooke maintained his position as calmly as though they were merely discussing last year's weather, ending with his usual pleasant nod. It was an infuriating kind of obstinacy.

“Good God!” exclaimed Sir James, with all the passion he was capable of. “Let's find him a position; let's spend some money on him. He could join a colonial governor's staff! Grampus might take him—and I could write to Fulke about it.”

“But Ladislaw won't let himself be shipped off like livestock, my dear fellow. He has his own ideas. I believe that if he left me tomorrow, you'd only hear more about him in the district. With his gift for public speaking and drafting documents, few men could match him as an agitator—an agitator, you know.”
“Agitator!” Sir James repeated bitterly. He felt that pronouncing each syllable with the right emphasis was enough to expose how hateful the thing was.

“But let's be reasonable, Chettam. Now, Dorothea. As you say, she ought to go to Celia as soon as she can. She can stay in your house, and meanwhile matters may settle down quietly. Let's not rush to fire our guns, you know. Standish will keep this to himself, and the news will be old before anyone hears it. Twenty things might take Ladislaw away without any action on my part, you know.”
“So I must understand that you refuse to do anything?”
“Refuse, Chettam? No—I didn't say refuse. I simply can't see what I could do. Ladislaw is a gentleman.”
“I'm glad to hear it!” said Sir James, irritated enough to forget his manners a little. “Casaubon certainly wasn't.”
“Well, it would have been worse if he'd added a codicil preventing her from ever marrying again, you know.”
“I'm not so sure,” said Sir James. “That would have shown more delicacy.”
“Just one of poor Casaubon's eccentricities! That attack affected his brain a little. None of it matters. She doesn't _want_ to marry Ladislaw.”

“But the codicil is worded to make everyone believe she did. I believe nothing of the kind about Dorothea,” said Sir James. Then he frowned. “But I distrust Ladislaw. I'll say it plainly: I distrust Ladislaw.”

“I couldn't act immediately on those grounds, Chettam. Indeed, even if we could pack him off—send him to Norfolk Island, something of that sort—it would make Dorothea look worse to anyone who knew about it. It would suggest we didn't trust her—didn't trust her, you know.”
Mr. Brooke's discovery of an unanswerable argument did nothing to calm Sir James. He reached for his hat, signalling that he would argue no further, and said, still heatedly—
“Well, all I can say is that Dorothea has already been sacrificed once because her friends failed to take enough care. As her brother, I'll do everything I can to protect her now.”

“The best thing you can do is bring her to Freshitt as soon as possible, Chettam. I'm entirely in favour of that plan,” said Mr. Brooke, pleased to have won the argument. Parting with Ladislaw just then would have been extremely inconvenient. Parliament might be dissolved any day, and the voters needed persuading which course would best serve the country's interests. Mr. Brooke honestly believed those interests would be served by electing him to Parliament. He sincerely offered the powers of his mind to the nation.

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter L
paragraphs:
“This Loller here wol precilen us somewhat.”
“Nay by my father’s soule! that schal he nat,”
Sayde the Schipman, ‘here schal he not preche,
We schal no gospel glosen here ne teche.
We leven all in the gret God,’ quod he.
He wolden sowen some diffcultee.”—_Canterbury Tales_.

Dorothea had been safely installed at Freshitt Hall for nearly a week before she asked any dangerous questions. Each morning she now sat with Celia in the prettiest of the upstairs sitting rooms, which opened into a small conservatory. Dressed in white and lavender, like a bunch of mixed violets, Celia watched her baby's remarkable activities. To her inexperienced mind they were so mysterious that she kept interrupting every conversation to ask the all-knowing nurse to interpret them. Beside her sat Dorothea in mourning, looking far too sad for Celia's liking. After all, the baby was perfectly well; and really, when a husband had been so tedious and troublesome alive, and had besides—well, well! Sir James had, of course, told Celia everything, impressing on her how important it was to keep Dorothea ignorant until telling her became unavoidable.

But Mr. Brooke had correctly predicted that Dorothea would not remain inactive for long when responsibilities had been given to her. She knew the substance of the will her husband had made at their marriage. As soon as she clearly understood her situation, she began quietly considering her duties as owner of Lowick Manor, including her right to appoint the parish clergyman.
One morning her uncle came for his customary visit, though in unusually lively spirits. He explained that it was now almost certain Parliament would be dissolved immediately. Dorothea said—

“Uncle, I ought now to consider who should have the living at Lowick. Once Mr. Tucker had been provided for, I never heard my husband mention any clergyman he had in mind to succeed him. I think I should have the keys now and go to Lowick to examine his papers. Something there may help me understand his wishes.”

“There's no hurry, my dear,” Mr. Brooke said calmly. “You can go later, if you wish. But I looked through the desks and drawers—there was nothing—nothing except learned subjects, you know—and the will. Everything can wait. As for the living, I've already been asked to use my influence—a rather good candidate, I should say. Mr. Tyke has been recommended to me very strongly. I helped obtain an appointment for him before. An apostolic man, I believe—the sort of person who would suit you, my dear.”

“I'd like to know more about him, uncle, and decide for myself, if Mr. Casaubon has left no indication of his wishes. Perhaps he added something to the will—there may be instructions for me,” said Dorothea. Throughout their conversation she had been thinking of this possibility in connection with her husband's work.
“Nothing about the rectory, my dear—nothing,” said Mr. Brooke. Getting up to leave, he held out his hand to his nieces. “Nor about his research, you know. Nothing in the will.”
Dorothea's lip began to tremble.
“Come, my dear, you mustn't think about these things yet. Later on, you know.”
“I'm quite well again, uncle. I want to do something.”

“Well, well, we'll see. But I must hurry off—there's no end to my work just now. It's a crisis—a political crisis, you know. And here's Celia with her little man—you're an aunt now, you know, and I'm a sort of grandfather,” said Mr. Brooke in a placid rush. He was eager to get away and tell Chettam it would not be his fault if Dorothea insisted on examining everything.
When her uncle had gone, Dorothea sank back into her chair and looked thoughtfully down at her folded hands.
“Look, Dodo! Look at him! Have you ever seen anything like it?” said Celia, in her contented, clipped way.
“What is it, Kitty?” Dorothea asked, raising her eyes rather absently.

“What? His upper lip, of course. Look how he's pulling it down, as though he were going to make a face. Isn't it wonderful! Perhaps he's having his own little thoughts. I wish nurse were here. Do look.”
A large tear, which had been gathering for some time, rolled down Dorothea's cheek as she raised her eyes and tried to smile.
“Don't be sad, Dodo. Kiss the baby. What are you brooding about? I'm sure you did everything—even far too much. You ought to be happy now.”
“I wonder whether Sir James would drive me to Lowick. I want to search through everything—to see whether any words were left for me.”

“You mustn't go until Mr. Lydgate gives permission, and he hasn't yet. Here you are, nurse: take baby and walk up and down the gallery. Besides, Dodo, you've got a mistaken idea in your head as usual. I can see it, and it upsets me.”

“What have I got wrong, Kitty?” Dorothea asked meekly. She was now almost prepared to believe that Celia was wiser than herself, and wondered with real anxiety what her mistaken idea might be. Celia recognized her advantage and meant to use it. None of the others knew Dodo as well as she did, or understood how to manage her. Since her baby's birth, Celia had gained a new confidence in her own sound judgment and calm wisdom. It seemed obvious that where there was a baby, matters were satisfactory, and that error in general was simply the absence of that central balancing force.

“I can see exactly what you're thinking, Dodo,” Celia said. “You're trying to discover whether there's something unpleasant you ought to do now, simply because Mr. Casaubon wanted it. As though you hadn't been uncomfortable enough already. And he doesn't deserve it, as you'll find out. He's behaved very badly. James is absolutely furious with him. I'd better tell you, to prepare you.”

“Celia,” Dorothea pleaded, “you're distressing me. Please tell me at once what you mean.” The thought flashed through her mind that Mr. Casaubon had left his property to someone else—which would not be so very distressing.
“Well, he's added a codicil to his will, saying you'd lose all the property if you married—I mean—”
“That doesn't matter at all,” Dorothea interrupted impulsively.

“But if you married Mr. Ladislaw, not anyone else,” Celia continued with unshakable calm. “Of course, in one sense that doesn't matter—you never _would_ marry Mr. Ladislaw. But that makes Mr. Casaubon's behaviour worse.”

Dorothea's face and neck flushed painfully. Celia, however, believed she was administering a sobering dose of reality. It was filling her head with ideas that had damaged Dodo's health so badly. So she continued in the same neutral voice, as if discussing the baby's clothes.

“James says so. He says it's abominable and quite unworthy of a gentleman. And nobody could judge better than James. It's as though Mr. Casaubon wanted people to believe you'd wish to marry Mr. Ladislaw—which is ridiculous. Only James says it was meant to stop Mr. Ladislaw wanting to marry you for your money—as if he'd ever think of proposing to you. Mrs. Cadwallader said you might as well marry an Italian with white mice! But I must just see how baby's doing,” Celia added in precisely the same tone. She threw a light shawl round her shoulders and tripped away.

By now Dorothea had gone cold again. She fell helplessly back in her chair. She might have described her experience as a vague, frightened awareness that her life was taking a new shape: she was undergoing a transformation in which memory could not adapt itself to the movement of newly formed organs. Everything looked different—her husband's behaviour, her sense of duty towards him, every conflict between them, and above all her entire relationship with Will Ladislaw. Her world was changing convulsively. The only clear thought she could form was that she must wait and think it all through again. One change frightened her as if it were a sin: a violent surge of revulsion from her dead husband, who had harboured secret thoughts, perhaps distorting everything she said and did. Then she felt another change, which also made her tremble—a sudden, unfamiliar longing for Will Ladislaw. It had never occurred to her that he might, under any circumstances, be her lover. Imagine the effect of suddenly learning that someone else had thought of him in that role—that perhaps he himself had recognized the possibility. And with that revelation came a rushing, jostling vision of unsuitable circumstances and questions that could not quickly be answered.

It seemed a long time—she could not tell how long—before she heard Celia saying, “That will do, nurse. He'll sit quietly on my lap now. You can have your lunch, and leave Garratt in the next room. What I think, Dodo,” Celia continued, noticing only that Dorothea was leaning back in her chair and looked unlikely to resist, “is that Mr. Casaubon was spiteful. I never liked him, nor did James. The corners of his mouth always looked dreadfully spiteful to me. And now he's behaved like this, I'm sure religion doesn't require you to make yourself miserable over him. If he's been taken away, it's a mercy, and you ought to be grateful. We shouldn't grieve, should we, baby?” Celia confided this to the unconscious centre and balancing point of the world. His fists were extraordinary, complete down to the fingernails; and when his cap came off, he really had enough hair to make—you couldn't say what. In short, he was a Western incarnation of Buddha.

At this critical moment Lydgate was announced. Almost his first words were, “I'm afraid you're not as well as you were, Mrs. Casaubon. Has something upset you? May I feel your pulse?” Dorothea's hand was as cold as marble.
“She wants to go to Lowick and examine papers,” said Celia. “She shouldn't, should she?”

For a moment Lydgate said nothing. Then, looking at Dorothea, he answered, “I'm not quite sure. I think Mrs. Casaubon ought to do whatever will give her the greatest peace of mind. Preventing her from acting won't always bring that peace.”

“Thank you,” said Dorothea, making an effort. “I'm sure you're right. There are so many things I ought to attend to. Why should I sit here doing nothing?” Trying to summon up subjects unconnected with her distress, she added abruptly, “I think you know everyone in Middlemarch, Mr. Lydgate. I'll have a great many questions for you. I have serious responsibilities now. I must appoint someone to a living. You know Mr. Tyke and all the—” But the effort was more than Dorothea could manage. She stopped and burst into tears.
Lydgate had her drink a dose of sal volatile, the restorative spirit.
Before leaving, he asked to speak to Sir James. “Let Mrs. Casaubon do what she wants,” he told him. “I think complete freedom is the treatment she needs most.”

Treating Dorothea during her mental agitation had allowed him to reach some accurate conclusions about the difficulties of her life. He was certain she had suffered from the strain and inner conflict of suppressing herself. Now she was likely to feel that she had merely exchanged one enclosure for another.

It became easier for Sir James to follow Lydgate's advice when he discovered that Celia had already told Dorothea the unpleasant truth about the will. Nothing could be done about that now, and there was no reason to postpone necessary business any longer. The following day, when Dorothea asked him to drive her to Lowick, he agreed at once.

“I don't want to stay there just yet,” Dorothea said. “I could hardly bear it. I'm much happier at Freshitt with Celia. Looking at Lowick from a distance will help me think more clearly about what should be done there. And I'd like to spend a little time with my uncle at the Grange, walking along all the old paths and visiting the people in the village.”

“Not yet, I think. Your uncle is entertaining political guests, and you're better away from all that,” said Sir James, who was thinking of the Grange chiefly as a place young Ladislaw frequented. Neither he nor Dorothea mentioned the offensive clause in the will; both felt that speaking of it to each other would be impossible. Sir James was reluctant to discuss disagreeable matters even with other men. As for Dorothea, the one thing she would have chosen to say was something she could not bring herself to mention yet, because it would further expose her husband's injustice. Still, she wished Sir James could know what she and her husband had said about Will Ladislaw's moral claim to the property. Then, she thought, he would see as clearly as she did that her husband's strange, indelicate condition sprang chiefly from his bitter resistance to that claim, and not simply from more intimate feelings that were harder to discuss. Admittedly, Dorothea also wanted this known for Will's sake, since her friends seemed to regard him only as a recipient of Mr. Casaubon's charity. Why compare him to an Italian carrying white mice? Those words of Mrs. Cadwallader's seemed a mocking caricature sketched in darkness by a malicious imp.

At Lowick, Dorothea searched every desk and drawer, every place where her husband had kept private papers. She found nothing addressed specifically to her except the “Synoptical Tabulation,” probably the first of many intended instructions. In arranging this legacy of work for Dorothea, as in everything else, Mr. Casaubon had proceeded slowly and hesitantly. Planning how to pass on his work had oppressed him just as doing it had: he felt he was laboriously moving through something dark and obstructive. His doubts about Dorothea's ability to arrange his materials were overcome only by his doubts about any other editor. Eventually, however, he had built himself a hope from Dorothea's character. What she resolved to do, she could accomplish; and he readily pictured her labouring, bound by a promise, to build a tomb bearing his name. Not that Mr. Casaubon called the projected volumes a tomb: he called them the Key to all Mythologies. But the months overtook him and his plans fell behind. He had found time only to ask for the promise through which he hoped to maintain his cold grip on Dorothea's life.

That grip had loosened.
