“His heart
The lowliest duties on itself did lay.”
—WORDSWORTH.

On the June evening when Mr. Farebrother learned that the Lowick living was his, joy filled the old-fashioned parlour. Even the portraits of the great lawyers seemed to look on approvingly. His mother left her tea and toast untouched. She sat with her customary pretty primness, revealing her feelings only through flushed cheeks and shining eyes—that touching, fleeting resemblance an old woman can suddenly bear to her distant younger self. She said firmly—
“The greatest comfort, Camden, is knowing you've earned it.”

“When a man gets a good position, mother, he has to earn half of it afterwards,” her son replied, overflowing with pleasure and making no attempt to hide it. His happiness had an active quality. It seemed energetic enough not merely to shine from his face, but to illuminate busy visions within. His glances appeared full of thoughts as well as delight.

“Now, aunt,” he continued, rubbing his hands and turning to Miss Noble, who was making soft little noises like a beaver, “there'll always be sugar-candy on the table for you to steal for the children. And you'll have any number of new stockings to give away, while you darn your own more than ever!”
Miss Noble nodded at her nephew with a quiet, slightly frightened laugh. On the strength of his advancement, she had already slipped another lump of sugar into her basket.
“As for you, Winny,” the Vicar continued, “I shan't object to your marrying any bachelor in Lowick—Mr. Solomon Featherstone, for instance—as soon as I discover you're in love with him.”

Miss Winifred had been gazing at her brother and weeping freely all this time; that was how she expressed joy. Smiling through her tears, she said, “You must show me how, Cam. _You_ must get married now.”
“Gladly! But who's in love with me? I'm a shabby old fellow,” said the Vicar. He stood, pushed back his chair and looked himself over. “What do you think, mother?”
“You're a handsome man, Camden, though your father cut a finer figure,” the old lady answered.
“I wish you'd marry Miss Garth, brother,” said Miss Winifred. “She'd make life at Lowick so cheerful.”

“Very fine! You speak as though young women were tied up for us to choose from, like poultry at a market—as though I had only to ask and anyone would accept me,” said the Vicar, choosing to name no particular woman.
“We don't want just anyone,” Miss Winifred replied. “But _you'd_ like Miss Garth, wouldn't you, mother?”

“Whoever my son chooses will be my choice,” said Mrs. Farebrother with stately discretion. “A wife would be very welcome, Camden. You'll want to play whist at home when we move to Lowick, and Henrietta Noble has never been a whist player.” Mrs. Farebrother invariably bestowed that magnificent name on her tiny old sister.
“I won't need whist any longer, mother.”

“Why ever not, Camden? In my day, whist was considered a perfectly proper amusement for a good churchman,” said Mrs. Farebrother. She knew nothing of what whist meant to her son, and spoke rather sharply, as though he were dangerously encouraging some new doctrine.
“I'll be too busy for it. I'll have two parishes,” the Vicar replied, preferring not to debate the game's virtues.

He had already told Dorothea, “I don't consider myself obliged to give up St. Botolph's. If I give someone else most of its income, that's enough of a protest against the practice of holding several livings, which they're trying to reform. Using power well takes more strength than surrendering it.”

“I've thought about that,” Dorothea said. “For one's own sake, I think giving up power and money would be easier than keeping them. It seems quite inappropriate that I should control this appointment, yet I felt I ought not to let someone else exercise the right for me.”
“Then it's my responsibility to act in a way that won't make you regret having that power,” said Mr. Farebrother.

His was a nature whose conscience became more active when life's burdens stopped chafing. He made no show of humility about it, but privately felt rather ashamed. His conduct had included lapses which others, who received no comfortable livings, had avoided.

“I often used to wish I'd chosen something other than the Church,” he told Lydgate. “But perhaps I'd do better to make myself as good a clergyman as I can. That's the comfortably provided clergyman's view, you see,” he finished with a smile. “It makes difficulties much simpler.”

At that moment the Vicar really did feel his duties would be easy. But Duty has a habit of behaving unexpectedly—rather like a heavy friend we have cordially invited to stay, who then breaks his leg inside our gates.
Scarcely a week later, Duty appeared in his study disguised as Fred Vincy, home from Omnibus College with his bachelor's degree.

“I'm ashamed to trouble you, Mr. Farebrother,” Fred said, his fair, open face asking indulgence. “But you're the only friend I can turn to for advice. I told you everything before, and you were so kind that I can't help coming back.”
“Sit down, Fred. I'll listen, and help in any way I can,” said the Vicar. He continued packing the small objects he was preparing for the move.

“I wanted to tell you—” Fred hesitated, then plunged ahead. “I could enter the Church now. Honestly, wherever I look, I can't see anything else I could do. I don't like the idea, but I know it's terribly hard on my father to say that after he's spent so much on educating me for it.” He paused again, then repeated, “And I can't see anything else I could do.”
“I did speak to your father about it, Fred, but I got nowhere. He said it was too late. Still, you've crossed one bridge now. What other difficulties stand in your way?”

“Only that I don't like it. I don't like theology, or preaching, or having to look solemn. I enjoy riding across country and doing what other men do. I don't mean I want to behave badly in any way. I simply have no taste for the things people expect from a clergyman. But what else is there? My father can't give me any capital, or I could take up farming. There's no place for me in his business. And obviously I can't begin studying law or medicine now, when he needs me to earn something. People say I ought not to enter the Church, but they might as well tell me to head off into the wilderness.”
Fred's voice had become a complaining protest. Mr. Farebrother might have smiled if he had not been so occupied with imagining what Fred had left unsaid.
“Do you have any doubts about doctrine—about the Articles?” he asked, making a determined effort to consider the question solely in Fred's interests.

“No. I suppose the Articles are right. I haven't any arguments against them, and much better, cleverer men than me accept them completely. I'd feel rather ridiculous claiming scruples of that kind, as though I were qualified to judge,” Fred said simply.
“Then I imagine you've considered that you might make a decent parish priest without being much of a theologian?”
“Of course, if I have to be a clergyman, I'll try to do my duty, even if I don't enjoy it. Do you think anyone ought to blame me?”

“For entering the Church in these circumstances? That depends on your conscience, Fred—on how thoroughly you've weighed the cost and understood what the position will demand. All I can say about myself is that I've always been too lax, and it has troubled me.”

“There's another difficulty,” Fred said, flushing. “I didn't tell you before, although perhaps some things I said made you guess. There's someone I'm very fond of. I've loved her since we were children.”
“Miss Garth, I assume?” said the Vicar, studying some labels intently.
“Yes. If she'd have me, I wouldn't mind anything. I know I could be a good fellow then.”
“And you believe she feels the same?”

“She won't ever say so. Some time ago she made me promise not to bring it up again. And she's particularly opposed to my becoming a clergyman—I know that much. But I can't give her up. I really do think she cares for me. I saw Mrs. Garth last night. She said Mary was staying with Miss Farebrother at Lowick Rectory.”
“Yes, she's kindly helping my sister. Would you like to go there?”
“No. I want to ask you an enormous favour. I'm ashamed to bother you like this, but Mary might listen if you spoke to her about it—about my entering the Church, I mean.”
“That's a delicate undertaking, my dear Fred. I would have to assume your attachment to her, and approaching the matter as you wish would amount to asking whether she returns your feelings.”
“That's exactly what I want her to tell you,” Fred said bluntly. “Until I know how she feels, I don't know what to do.”
“You mean her answer would guide your decision about entering the Church?”
“If Mary said she'd never have me, I might as well go wrong one way as another.”
“That's nonsense, Fred. Men survive their love, but they don't outlive the consequences of reckless behaviour.”
“Not love like mine. I can't remember a time when I didn't love Mary. Giving her up would be like learning to live on wooden legs.”
“Might she resent my interference?”

“No, I'm certain she wouldn't. She respects you more than anyone. She wouldn't put you off with jokes, the way she does me. I couldn't have told anyone else, of course, or asked anyone but you to speak to her. Nobody else could be such a friend to us both.” Fred paused, then added rather plaintively, “And she ought to recognize that I worked to pass my degree. She ought to believe I'd make an effort for her.”
There was a brief silence. Then Mr. Farebrother set down his work and held out his hand to Fred.
“All right, my boy. I'll do as you ask.”
That same day Mr. Farebrother rode to Lowick parsonage on the horse he had recently acquired. “Clearly I'm an old stem,” he thought. “The young shoots are pushing me aside.”

He found Mary in the garden, collecting roses and scattering their petals over a sheet. The sun was sinking, and tall trees cast shadows across the grassy paths where she walked without a bonnet or parasol. She did not notice the Vicar approaching over the grass. She had just bent to scold a small black-and-tan terrier which insisted on walking over the sheet and sniffing the petals as she dropped them. Holding his front paws in one hand, she raised a finger of the other. The dog wrinkled his forehead and looked embarrassed. “Fly, Fly, I'm ashamed of you,” Mary was saying in her deep, serious voice. “This isn't how a sensible dog behaves. Anyone would think you were a foolish young gentleman.”
“You show young gentlemen no mercy, Miss Garth,” said the Vicar, now only two yards away.
Mary straightened abruptly and blushed. “Reasoning with Fly always works,” she said with a laugh.
“But reasoning with young gentlemen doesn't?”
“With some, I suppose. After all, some grow into excellent men.”
“I'm pleased you'll admit that, because I've come to interest you in a young gentleman myself.”
“Not a foolish one, I hope,” said Mary, returning to her roses. Her heart had begun beating uncomfortably.

“No. Though perhaps wisdom isn't his greatest strength—affection and sincerity are. Still, those two qualities contain more wisdom than people generally suppose. I hope that description tells you who I mean.”
“Yes, I think so,” Mary answered bravely. Her expression grew more serious and her hands turned cold. “You must mean Fred Vincy.”
“He's asked me to consult you about entering the Church. I hope you won't think I presumed too much by agreeing.”
“Quite the opposite, Mr. Farebrother,” said Mary. She stopped picking roses and folded her arms, but could not raise her eyes. “Whenever you have something to say to me, I feel honoured.”

“Before we discuss that, though, let me mention something your father told me in confidence. It was, incidentally, the very evening I last carried a message from Fred, just after he'd gone back to college. Mr. Garth told me what happened on the night Featherstone died—your refusal to burn the will. He said your conscience troubled you because you had innocently prevented Fred from receiving his ten thousand pounds. I've remembered that. And I've learned something that may ease your mind—that may show you there's no need for a sin-offering on that account.”

Mr. Farebrother paused and looked at her. He meant to give Fred every advantage. But he thought it best to clear her mind of the superstitious feelings that sometimes lead women to wrong a man by marrying him as an act of atonement. Mary's cheeks had begun to burn, and she said nothing.

“What I mean is that your action made no actual difference to Fred's prospects. I've learned that burning the later will wouldn't have made the earlier one legally valid. If challenged, it wouldn't have stood—and you can be certain it would have been challenged. On that point, then, you can set your mind at rest.”
“Thank you, Mr. Farebrother,” Mary said earnestly. “I'm very grateful that you remembered how I felt.”

“Now I can go on. As you know, Fred has his degree. He's worked his way that far, and must now decide what to do. The question is so difficult that he's inclined to follow his father's wishes and enter the Church, although you know better than I how strongly he used to oppose it. I've questioned him, and I admit that, as things stand, I see no insurmountable objection to his becoming a clergyman. He says he could set himself to doing his best in that calling, on one condition. If that condition were met, I'd do everything I could to help him advance. In time—not immediately, of course—he could become my curate. There would be enough work for him that his salary would almost equal what I used to receive as Vicar. But, as I say, all this depends on one condition. He has confided in me, Miss Garth, and asked me to speak for him. That condition rests entirely on your feelings.”

Mary seemed so deeply affected that he paused, then said, “Shall we walk a little?” As they walked he added, “To put it plainly, Fred won't do anything that might reduce his chance of your agreeing to marry him. But with that hope, he'll do his best at any work you approve of.”

“I couldn't possibly promise ever to marry him, Mr. Farebrother. But I certainly never will if he becomes a clergyman. Your proposal is immensely kind and generous. I wouldn't dream of questioning your judgment. It's only my girlish habit of seeing things in a mocking light,” Mary said. A playful sparkle returned to her answer, making its modesty still more charming.
“He wants me to tell him exactly what you think,” Mr. Farebrother replied.

“I couldn't love a ridiculous man,” said Mary, choosing not to go deeper. “Fred has enough knowledge and common sense to earn respect in some useful worldly occupation, if he chooses. But I can't picture him preaching, exhorting, pronouncing blessings or praying beside the sick without feeling I'm looking at a caricature. He'd enter the Church only for social standing, and nothing seems more contemptible to me than that sort of feeble-minded gentility. I used to feel the same about Mr. Crowse, with his vacant face, tidy umbrella and fussy little speeches. What right have men like that to represent Christianity—as though it were an institution for dressing idiots respectably—as though—” Mary stopped herself. She had been carried away as if speaking to Fred rather than Mr. Farebrother.
“Young women judge harshly. They don't experience the pressure of action as men do—though perhaps I ought to except you. But surely you don't place Fred Vincy as low as that?”
“Certainly not. He has plenty of sense. But I don't think it would show if he became a clergyman. He'd be playing at a profession.”
“So your answer is definite? As a clergyman, he'd have no hope?”
Mary answered with a shake of her head.
“But suppose he faced all the difficulties of earning his living in another way. Would you give him hope to sustain him? Could he count on winning you?”

“I don't think Fred needs to be told again what I've already said,” Mary replied with a trace of resentment. “I mean he shouldn't ask these questions until he's actually done something worthwhile, instead of saying he could.”

Mr. Farebrother remained silent for a minute or more. Then they turned and stopped beneath a maple's shade at the end of a grassy path, and he said, “I understand that you resist any attempt to bind you. But either your feeling for Fred Vincy prevents you from becoming attached to someone else, or it doesn't. Either he can rely on your remaining unmarried until he's earned your hand, or he may be disappointed whatever he does. Forgive me, Mary—you know I used to question you on your catechism by that name. But when a woman's affections affect the happiness of another life—of more than one life—I think the nobler course is complete openness and honesty.”

Now Mary was silent. It was not Mr. Farebrother's manner that puzzled her, but his tone, with its grave, restrained emotion. The strange possibility flashed through her mind that he was referring to himself. She could not believe it, and felt ashamed even to imagine it. She had never supposed any man could love her except Fred, who had married her with a ring from an umbrella when she still wore little socks and strapped shoes. Still less had she imagined that she might matter to Mr. Farebrother, the cleverest man in her small circle. She had only time to sense how uncertain and perhaps illusory all this was. One thing, however, was clear and settled: her answer.

“Since you think it's my duty, Mr. Farebrother, I'll tell you: my feelings for Fred are too strong for me to give him up for anyone else. I could never be entirely happy knowing he was unhappy because he'd lost me. My gratitude to him is rooted so deeply—for always loving me best, and caring so much whenever I hurt myself, ever since we were tiny. I can't imagine any new feeling weakening that. More than anything, I'd like to see him deserve everyone's respect. But please tell him I won't promise to marry him before then. It would shame and grieve my father and mother. He's free to choose someone else.”

“Then I've fully carried out my commission,” said Mr. Farebrother, offering Mary his hand. “I'll ride straight back to Middlemarch. With that hope before him, we'll find Fred his proper place somehow. And I hope I'll live to join your hands. God bless you!”

“Oh, do stay and let me give you some tea,” Mary pleaded. Tears filled her eyes. Something she could not name in his manner—something like a resolute effort to suppress pain—made her suddenly miserable, as she had once been on seeing her father's hands tremble in distress.
“No, my dear, no. I must go back.”
Three minutes later the Vicar was on his horse again. He had generously fulfilled a duty far harder than giving up whist, or even writing penitential meditations.

chapters.title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter LIII
paragraphs:
It is but a shallow haste which concludeth insincerity from what
outsiders call inconsistency—putting a dead mechanism of “ifs” and
“therefores” for the living myriad of hidden suckers whereby the belief
and the conduct are wrought into mutual sustainment.

As Mr. Bulstrode hoped to acquire property in Lowick, he naturally had a particular wish that its new clergyman should be someone he fully approved of. Instead, just as he received the deeds making him owner of Stone Court, Mr. Farebrother formally assumed his duties in the quaint little church and preached his first sermon to the farmers, labourers and village craftsmen. Bulstrode understood this as punishment and warning for his own failings and those of the nation. He had no immediate intention of attending Lowick Church or living at Stone Court. He had bought the excellent farm and fine house simply as a retreat. Gradually he could add land and improve the dwelling, until taking up residence there would serve God's glory. He could then withdraw partly from his business activities and place the influence of a local landowner more conspicuously behind Gospel truth. Providence might increase that influence through unexpected opportunities to purchase more land. The surprising ease with which he had obtained Stone Court seemed a strong divine guidance in this direction. Everyone had expected Mr. Rigg Featherstone to hold on to it as though it were Eden. Poor old Peter had expected as much himself. In imagination he had often gazed up through the turf above his grave and, unhindered by perspective, watched his frog-faced heir enjoying the fine old estate, to the perpetual astonishment and disappointment of the other survivors.

Yet how little we know what paradise would mean to our neighbours! We judge by our own wishes, and our neighbours do not always reveal even a hint of theirs. Cool, calculating Joshua Rigg had never allowed his father to suspect that Stone Court was anything less than his highest ambition; and he certainly had wanted to own it. But just as Warren Hastings looked at gold and thought of buying Daylesford, Joshua Rigg looked at Stone Court and thought of buying gold. His vision of supreme happiness was both precise and intense. Circumstances had given the vigorous greed he inherited a particular shape: he longed to be a moneychanger. Ever since his first employment as an errand boy in a seaport, he had gazed through moneychangers' windows as other boys gazed into pastry shops. The fascination had gradually become a deep, exclusive passion. Once wealthy, he intended to do many things, including marry a genteel young woman; but these were incidental pleasures, dispensable to his imagination. The one delight his soul thirsted for was a moneychanger's shop on a busy quay. He would sit surrounded by locks to which he alone held the keys, looking supremely cool as he handled the multiplying coins of every nation, while helpless Greed stared enviously through an iron grille. That passion had given him the strength to master all the knowledge needed to satisfy it. While others imagined he had settled at Stone Court for life, Joshua was thinking how soon he might settle on the North Quay, equipped with the finest safes and locks.

Enough of that. Our concern is Joshua Rigg's sale as Mr. Bulstrode saw it. He interpreted it as an encouraging act of Providence, perhaps endorsing a purpose he had long entertained without outward encouragement. He did so cautiously, however, framing his thanksgiving in guarded terms. His doubts had nothing to do with what the event might mean for Joshua Rigg's destiny. That belonged to unmapped territory outside Providence's government, except perhaps under some imperfect colonial administration. Rather, Bulstrode reflected that this event too might be meant to chastise him, just as Mr. Farebrother's appointment plainly was.

This was not something Mr. Bulstrode told other people to deceive them. It was what he told himself. It was as sincerely his explanation of events as any theory of yours, if you disagree with him, may be yours. The self-interest mixed into our theories does not make them insincere. Indeed, the more they satisfy our self-interest, the firmer our belief becomes.

Whether as approval or punishment, then, Mr. Bulstrode became owner of Stone Court barely fifteen months after Peter Featherstone's death. What Peter would say “if he were worthy to know” became an endless, comforting topic among his disappointed relatives. The tables had turned on their dear departed brother. Solomon never tired of savouring how the cunning of circumstances had defeated Peter's own cunning. Mrs. Waule enjoyed a melancholy triumph in this proof that inventing false Featherstones and disinheriting the true ones did not pay. When Sister Martha heard the news in the Chalky Flats, she said, “Dear, dear! Then the Almighty can't have been so pleased with those almshouses after all.”

Affectionate Mrs. Bulstrode was especially pleased by the benefit Stone Court might bring her husband's health. Hardly a day passed without his riding over to inspect some part of the farm with the bailiff. Evenings in that quiet place were delightful. Newly built hayricks scented the air, mingling with the fragrance of the luxuriant old garden. One evening, while the sun still stood above the horizon, burning like golden lamps among the great walnut branches, Mr. Bulstrode waited on horseback outside the front gate for Caleb Garth. They had arranged to meet so Caleb could advise about drainage in the stables; he was now in the rickyard consulting with the bailiff.

Mr. Bulstrode felt spiritually well disposed and unusually peaceful, thanks to his innocent recreation. His religious doctrine assured him he possessed no merit whatever. Yet that conviction can be held painlessly when one's unworthiness takes no definite shape in memory, reviving the sting of shame or the ache of remorse. It can even bring intense satisfaction when the depth of our sins merely measures the depth of forgiveness and supplies conclusive proof that we are specially chosen instruments of God's purpose. Memory has as many moods as temperament, changing its scenery like a diorama. At this moment the sunlight seemed to Bulstrode continuous with that of distant evenings when, as a very young man, he used to go preaching beyond Highbury. He would gladly have looked forward to such a service of exhortation now. The texts still existed, and so did his skill at explaining them. Caleb Garth's return interrupted this brief reverie. Caleb too was mounted and had just shaken his bridle to set off when he exclaimed—
“Bless me! Who's this fellow in black coming down the lane? He looks like one of those men you see hanging about after the races.”

Mr. Bulstrode turned his horse to look down the lane but said nothing. The approaching figure was our slight acquaintance Mr. Raffles. Nothing about him had changed except his black suit and crape hatband. He came within three yards of the riders. They saw recognition flash across his face as he swung his stick up, keeping his eyes on Mr. Bulstrode, and finally cried—

“By Jove, Nick, it is you! No mistaking you, though twenty-five years have played the devil with us both! How are you, eh? You didn't expect to find _me_ here. Come on, shake hands.” Saying that Mr. Raffles was rather excited would merely have been another way of saying it was evening. Caleb Garth noticed a moment's struggle and hesitation in Mr. Bulstrode. Then the banker coldly held out his hand and said—
“I certainly did not expect to encounter you in this isolated country spot.”

“It belongs to my stepson,” said Raffles, adopting a swaggering stance. “I've visited him here before. I'm not so surprised to see you, old fellow, because I picked up a letter—what you might call an act of Providence. Still, it's remarkably lucky I've met you. I don't particularly want to see my stepson. He's not affectionate, and his poor mother's dead now. To tell the truth, Nick, it was love for you that brought me. I came for your address, because—look!” He pulled a crumpled paper from his pocket.

Almost anyone except Caleb Garth might have lingered to hear more. This man's acquaintance with Bulstrode suggested episodes in the banker's life so unlike anything Middlemarch knew of him that they promised the fascination of a secret. Caleb, however, was unusual. Some tendencies generally strong in human beings scarcely existed in him, including curiosity about other people's private affairs. If something discreditable might be discovered about a man, Caleb especially preferred not to know it. When he had to tell a subordinate that his misconduct had been found out, Caleb was more embarrassed than the offender. He now spurred his horse. “Good evening, Mr. Bulstrode. I must get home,” he said, and trotted off.

“You didn't give your full address on this letter,” Raffles continued. “Not like the first-rate businessman you used to be. ‘The Shrubs’—that could be anywhere. You live nearby, eh? Given up the London concern altogether? Turned country squire, perhaps, with a rural mansion to invite me to? Lord, what a lot of years! The old lady must have been dead a good while—gone to glory without the pain of learning how poor her daughter was, eh? But by Jove, Nick, you look pale and pasty. Come along, if you're heading home, I'll walk beside you.”

Mr. Bulstrode's habitual pallor had indeed become almost deathly. Five minutes earlier, the whole expanse of his life lay bathed in evening sunshine reaching back to the morning of memory. Sin had seemed a matter of doctrine and inward repentance; humiliation, a private exercise; the meaning of his actions, a question of inward vision shaped solely by spiritual relationships and ideas of God's purposes. Now, as if conjured by some hideous magic, this loud, red-faced figure stood solidly and uncontrollably before him—the past made flesh, in a form of punishment he had never imagined. But Mr. Bulstrode's mind was working, and he was not a man to speak or act rashly.
“I was on my way home,” he said, “but I can postpone my ride. You may rest here, if you wish.”
“Thank you,” Raffles replied with a grimace. “I don't care to see my stepson just now. I'd rather come home with you.”
“If you mean Mr. Rigg Featherstone, your stepson no longer lives here. This is now my property.”

Raffles widened his eyes and gave a long, surprised whistle. “Well then, no objection. I've walked quite far enough from the coach road. I've never been much of a walker—or a rider, for that matter. Give me a smart carriage and a spirited cob. I've always been a little heavy in the saddle. What a pleasant surprise seeing me must be, old fellow!” he went on as they turned towards the house. “You don't say so, but you never greeted your good fortune heartily. You were always thinking of improving the occasion—and you certainly had a gift for improving your luck.”
Mr. Raffles thoroughly enjoyed his own wit. He swung his leg with a swagger that rather strained his companion's carefully judged patience.

“If I remember correctly,” Mr. Bulstrode said with cold anger, “our acquaintance years ago was not as intimate as you now presume, Mr. Raffles. I shall be more willing to provide whatever assistance you seek if you avoid a familiarity that never characterized our former dealings, and which more than twenty years apart can hardly justify.”

“You don't like being called Nick? Why, in my heart I always called you Nick. Lost to sight, to memory dear! By Jove, my feelings for you have matured like fine old cognac. I hope there's some in the house. Josh filled my flask generously last time.”

Mr. Bulstrode had not yet fully grasped that Raffles's appetite for torment equalled even his appetite for cognac. Any sign of irritation simply gave him a fresh opening. But further objections were plainly useless. When Bulstrode instructed the housekeeper to accommodate his guest, he maintained a determined calm.
He could at least take comfort in knowing that this housekeeper had served Rigg too. She might suppose he was entertaining Raffles only as a friend of her former employer.
Once food and drink stood before the visitor in the panelled parlour, and nobody else remained in the room, Mr. Bulstrode said—

“Our habits differ so greatly, Mr. Raffles, that neither of us is likely to enjoy the other's company. The sensible course, therefore, is to part as soon as possible. Since you say you wanted to see me, I assume you had some business to discuss. In the circumstances, however, I invite you to stay here tonight. I shall ride over early tomorrow—before breakfast, in fact—and hear whatever you wish to communicate.”

“Gladly,” said Raffles. “It's comfortable here—a bit dull for a long stay, but I can manage one night with this good liquor and the prospect of seeing you again in the morning. You're a much better host than my stepson. Josh held a bit of a grudge because I married his mother. But there's never been anything between you and me except kindness.”

Hoping that drink accounted for much of Raffles's peculiar blend of jollity and sneering, Mr. Bulstrode decided to say no more until he was sober. Yet as he rode home he saw with terrible clarity how difficult it would be to reach any dependable, lasting arrangement with this man. Inevitably he wanted to be rid of John Raffles, though his return could not be considered outside God's plan. The spirit of evil might have sent him to threaten Bulstrode's usefulness as an instrument of good, but the threat must have been permitted. This was a new kind of chastisement. His anguish differed profoundly from those hours when his struggle had remained safely private, ending in the assurance that his hidden misdeeds were forgiven and his services accepted. Even when he committed those deeds, had they not been half sanctified by his single-minded wish to devote himself and all he possessed to advancing the divine design? Was he now, after all, to become merely a stumbling stone and rock of offence? Who would understand the work taking place within him? Given an excuse to disgrace him, who would not throw his whole life and the truths he upheld into one heap of condemnation?

In his most private reflections, lifelong habit dressed Mr. Bulstrode's most selfish fears in religious language about purposes beyond humanity. Yet even as we discuss the earth's orbit and the solar system, what we feel and guide our movements by is the solid ground and the changing daylight. Now, beneath the automatic procession of theoretical phrases, he anticipated disgrace before his neighbours and his own wife. That expectation was as inward and unmistakable as the shivering ache of an approaching fever while we discuss pain in the abstract. Both the suffering of disgrace and the public judgment of it depend on how much a man previously claimed to be. To men whose only aim is avoiding serious crime, nothing short of the prisoner's dock means disgrace. Mr. Bulstrode, however, had aspired to be an outstanding Christian.

It was only half past seven the next morning when he reached Stone Court again. The fine old place had never looked more inviting as a home. Great white lilies were blooming, and nasturtiums, their pretty leaves silvered with dew, trailed over the low stone wall. Even the surrounding sounds seemed to contain a peaceful heart. But for the owner, everything was spoiled as he paced the gravel outside, waiting for Mr. Raffles to come downstairs. He was condemned to breakfast with him.

Soon they sat together in the panelled parlour over tea and toast, all Raffles cared for at that hour. His morning self differed less from his evening self than Bulstrode had hoped. If anything, slightly lower spirits sharpened his pleasure in tormenting. Certainly his manners appeared more unpleasant in daylight.

“I have little time to spare, Mr. Raffles,” said the banker. He could scarcely do more than sip his tea and break his toast without eating it. “I should be obliged if you would state immediately why you wanted to see me. I assume you have a home elsewhere and will be glad to return to it.”

“Why, doesn't a man with any heart want to see an old friend, Nick? I must call you Nick. We always called you young Nick when we knew you meant to marry the old widow. Some said you bore a handsome family resemblance to Old Nick, but that was your mother's fault for naming you Nicholas. Aren't you pleased to see me? I'd expected an invitation to stay at some pretty place of yours. My own home's broken up since my wife died. I'm not particularly attached to anywhere. I'd settle hereabouts as readily as anywhere else.”
“May I ask why you came back from America? When you expressed such a strong desire to go, and were given sufficient money, I understood that as effectively a promise to remain there for life.”
“I never knew wanting to go somewhere meant wanting to stay. Still, I stayed about ten years. Staying longer didn't suit me. And I shan't go back, Nick.” Raffles looked at him and slowly winked.
“Do you want help setting up in business? What occupation do you follow now?”

“Thank you, my occupation is enjoying myself as much as possible. I don't care to work any more. If I did anything, it would be a little travelling in tobacco—or something similar that brings a man into pleasant company. But I'd need an independent income to fall back on. That's what I want. I'm not as strong as I used to be, Nick, though I've more colour than you. I want independence.”
“That could be provided, if you undertook to stay away,” Mr. Bulstrode said, perhaps with too much eagerness beneath his voice.

“That'll have to depend on my convenience,” Raffles replied coolly. “Why shouldn't I make a few acquaintances here? I'm not ashamed to keep company with anyone. I left my portmanteau at the turnpike when I got off the coach. A change of linen—genuine, on my honour—not just shirt fronts and cuffs. And in this mourning suit, trouser straps and all, I'd do you credit among the local gentry.” He pushed his chair back and examined himself, especially the straps. His main object was to annoy Bulstrode, but he genuinely believed his current appearance would impress. In his opinion he was handsome and witty, and his style of mourning suggested substantial family connections.
“If you mean to depend on me in any way, Mr. Raffles,” Bulstrode said after a pause, “you must expect to comply with my wishes.”

“Ah, naturally,” said Raffles with mocking warmth. “Didn't I always? Lord, you profited handsomely through me, and I received very little. I've often thought since that I might have done better by telling the old woman I'd found her daughter and grandchild. It would have suited my feelings better. I've a soft spot in my heart. But you've buried the old lady by now, I suppose, so it's all the same to her. And you've made your fortune from that profitable business that was so blessed. Now you're a gentleman, buying land and playing the country pasha. Still a Dissenter, eh? Still godly? Or have you joined the Church because it's more respectable?”

This time Raffles's slow wink and slightly protruding tongue were worse than a nightmare, precisely because Bulstrode knew this was no dream but waking misery. He felt a shuddering nausea and remained silent, earnestly weighing whether to let Raffles do as he pleased and simply denounce him as a slanderer. The fellow would soon prove disreputable enough that nobody would believe him. “Not if he tells an ugly truth about _you_,” his clearer consciousness answered. Besides, although keeping Raffles away seemed no wrong, Bulstrode recoiled from directly lying to deny true statements. Looking back at forgiven sins—or explaining questionable compliance with lax practices—was one thing. Deliberately committing himself to necessary falsehood was another.
Since Bulstrode said nothing, Raffles continued, making the fullest use of his time.

“By Jove, I've not had your luck! New York treated me damned badly. Those Yankees are cool customers. A man with gentlemanly feelings hasn't a chance against them. I married after I returned—a nice woman in the tobacco trade, very fond of me. But business was limited, as we say. A friend had set her up there years before. Unfortunately, there was one son too many. Josh and I never got along. Still, I made the best of things, and I've always had my drink in good company. I've kept everything above board. I'm open as daylight. You won't hold it against me that I didn't find you sooner. I have a complaint that makes me rather slow about things. I thought you were still trading and praying away in London, but I couldn't find you there. You see, though, I was sent to you, Nick—perhaps as a blessing to us both.”

He ended with a comic nasal whine. Nobody felt more intellectually superior to religious cant than Raffles. And if cunning that calculates on people's basest feelings counts as intellect, he possessed his share. Beneath the blustering, teasing tone of his talk, his statements were evidently selected like moves in a chess game. Meanwhile Bulstrode had chosen his own move. Gathering his resolution, he said—

“You would do well to remember, Mr. Raffles, that a man can overreach himself in trying to gain an unfair advantage. I am under no obligation to you. Nevertheless, I am willing to provide a regular annuity, paid quarterly, for as long as you keep a promise to stay away from this neighbourhood. The choice is yours. If you insist on remaining here, even briefly, you will receive nothing from me. I shall refuse to acknowledge you.”
“Ha, ha!” Raffles burst out theatrically. “That reminds me of a comical thief who refused to acknowledge the constable.”
“Your insinuations have no bearing on me, sir,” Bulstrode said with white-hot anger. “Neither you nor anyone else can give the law a hold over me.”
“You can't take a joke, my good fellow. I only meant that _I'd_ never refuse to acknowledge _you_. But seriously, quarterly payments don't quite suit me. I like my freedom.”

Raffles stood and strode across the room once or twice, swinging his leg and adopting the air of a man reflecting with authority. At last he stopped before Bulstrode. “I'll tell you what. Give me a couple of hundred—come, that's modest—and I'll leave. On my honour! I'll collect my portmanteau and go. But I won't surrender my liberty for a miserable annuity. I'll come and go wherever I choose. Perhaps it'll suit me to stay away and correspond with a friend; perhaps it won't. Have you got the money on you?”
“No, only one hundred,” Bulstrode said. Immediate relief was too welcome to reject because the future remained uncertain. “Give me an address, and I'll send the rest.”
“No, I'll wait until you bring it,” said Raffles. “I'll take a walk and get something to eat. You'll be back by then.”

Bulstrode's weak body, shaken by everything he had endured since the previous evening, left him feeling utterly at the mercy of this loud, invulnerable man. Just then he grasped at temporary relief on any terms. He was rising to obey when Raffles raised a finger as though something had suddenly occurred to him.

“I did look for Sarah again, though I never told you. My conscience bothered me about that pretty young woman. I didn't find her, but I learned her husband's name and wrote it down. Then, damn it, I lost my pocketbook. Still, I'd recognize it if I heard it. My faculties are as good as in my prime, but names wear out, by Jove! Sometimes I'm no better than a damned tax form before the names are filled in. Anyway, if I hear of her or her family, I'll tell you, Nick. Now she's your stepdaughter, you'd like to help her.”
“Certainly,” said Mr. Bulstrode, his light-grey eyes as steady as usual. “Though that might limit my ability to assist you.”

As Bulstrode left, Raffles winked slowly at his retreating back. Then he turned to the window to watch the banker ride away, practically at his command. His lips curled into a smile, followed by a brief triumphant laugh.

“But what the devil was the name?” he soon muttered, scratching his head and drawing horizontal wrinkles across his forehead. He had not really cared about, or even considered, this lapse of memory until it occurred to him while inventing ways to torment Bulstrode.

“It began with L. Almost all l's, I fancy,” he continued, feeling the elusive name almost within reach. But his grasp was too slight, and he soon tired of the mental pursuit. Few men were less patient with solitary occupation, or more dependent on constantly making themselves heard, than Mr. Raffles. He preferred spending his time in pleasant conversation with the bailiff and housekeeper. From them he learned as much as he wanted about Bulstrode's standing in Middlemarch.

Even so, a dull interval eventually arose which required the relief of bread, cheese and ale. Sitting alone with these resources in the panelled parlour, Raffles suddenly slapped his knee and exclaimed, “Ladislaw!” The work of memory he had tried to initiate, then abandoned in despair, had suddenly completed itself without conscious effort. It is a common experience, as satisfying as a completed sneeze, even when the recovered name is worthless. Raffles immediately took out his pocketbook and wrote it down. He did not expect to use it; he simply wished to have it available if he ever needed it. He would not tell Bulstrode. Telling offered no immediate advantage, whereas to a mind like Raffles's a secret always held the prospect of one.

Satisfied with his success, by three that afternoon he had collected his portmanteau at the turnpike and boarded the coach. Mr. Bulstrode's view of Stone Court was cleared of an ugly black blot. But he was not freed from the fear that the blot might return and become inseparable even from his vision of his own hearth.

chapters.title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LIV
paragraphs:
“Negli occhi porta la mia donna Amore;
Per che si fa gentil ciò ch’ella mira:
Ov’ella passa, ogni uom ver lei si gira,
E cui saluta fa tremar lo core.
Sicchè, bassando il viso, tutto smore, E d’ogni suo difetto allor sospira: Fuggon dinanzi a lei Superbia ed Ira: Aiutatemi, donne, a farle onore.

Ogni dolcezza, ogni pensiero umile Nasce nel core a chi parlar la sente; Ond’è beato chi prima la vide. Quel ch’ella par quand’ un poco sorride, Non si può dicer, nè tener a mente, Si è nuovo miracolo gentile.” —DANTE: _La Vita Nuova_.

By that lovely morning when the Stone Court hayricks perfumed the air impartially, as though Mr. Raffles deserved the finest incense, Dorothea was living at Lowick Manor again. After three months, Freshitt had begun to feel oppressive. She could not spend hours every day posing like Saint Catherine, gazing ecstatically at Celia's baby. Yet a childless sister could hardly be allowed to remain in that momentous infant's presence while persistently ignoring him. Had there been a need, Dorothea would gladly have carried the baby a mile, loving him all the more tenderly for the effort. But an aunt who does not recognize her nephew as Buddha, and has nothing to do for him but admire him, is liable to find his behaviour repetitive and the pleasure of watching it exhaustible. Celia could not conceive of this. To her, Dorothea's childless widowhood fitted very prettily with little Arthur's birth—the baby had been named after Mr. Brooke.

“Dodo is just the sort of person who doesn't mind having nothing of her own—children or anything!” Celia told her husband. “And if she'd had a baby, it could never have been as sweet as Arthur. Could it, James?”
“Not if it resembled Casaubon,” Sir James answered. He knew he was answering indirectly, and kept strictly to himself his actual opinion of his firstborn's perfections.

“No! Just imagine! Really, it was a mercy,” said Celia. “I think being a widow is very nice for Dodo. She can love our baby as much as if he were hers, and have as many ideas of her own as she pleases.”
“It's a pity she wasn't a queen,” said the devoted Sir James.
“But then what would we have been? We'd have had to be something different,” Celia objected, disliking such a laborious effort of imagination. “I prefer her as she is.”

So when Celia discovered that Dorothea was arranging to return permanently to Lowick, her eyebrows rose in disappointment. In her quiet, unassuming manner, she launched a needle-sharp barb of sarcasm.

“What will you do at Lowick, Dodo? You say yourself there's nothing to do. Everyone is so clean and comfortable that it makes you positively melancholy. And you've been so happy here, going round all the worst backyards in Tipton with Mr. Garth. Now uncle's abroad, the two of you can do exactly as you please. And I'm sure James does everything you tell him.”
“I'll visit often, and I'll notice baby's growth all the better,” Dorothea replied.
“But you'll never see him being washed,” said Celia. “That's the best part of the day.” She was almost pouting. It seemed cruel of Dodo to leave the baby when she could stay.

“Dear Kitty, I'll come and spend the night especially,” said Dorothea. “But just now I want to be alone in my own home. I want to know the Farebrothers better, and talk to Mr. Farebrother about what can be done in Middlemarch.”

Dorothea's natural strength of will was no longer entirely channelled into determined submission. She longed to be at Lowick and had simply decided to go. She did not feel obliged to explain every reason. Everyone around her disapproved, however. Sir James was deeply distressed. He proposed that they should all move to Cheltenham for a few months, taking the sacred ark, otherwise known as a cradle. In those days, once Cheltenham had been rejected, a man scarcely knew what else to suggest.

The Dowager Lady Chettam had just returned from visiting her daughter in London. She wanted them at least to write to Mrs. Vigo and offer her the position of companion to Mrs. Casaubon. Surely a young widow like Dorothea could not mean to live alone at Lowick. Mrs. Vigo had served royal personages as reader and secretary. Even Dorothea could find no fault with her knowledge and principles.

Mrs. Cadwallader told her privately, “You'll certainly go mad alone in that house, my dear. You'll start seeing visions. We all have to make some effort to stay sane, and to call things by the names other people use. Of course, for younger sons and penniless women, madness is one way of being provided for: somebody looks after them then. But you mustn't resort to that. I dare say our good dowager bores you a little here. Still, think what a bore you might become to everyone else if you were always playing the tragic queen and treating everything sublimely. Sitting alone in that library, you might imagine you controlled the weather. You need a few people around who wouldn't believe you if you said so. That's a good medicine for bringing one down to earth.”
“I've never called everything by the same names as the people around me,” Dorothea said firmly.
“But I assume you've discovered your mistake, my dear,” Mrs. Cadwallader replied. “Which proves you're sane.”

Dorothea recognized the sting, but it did not wound her. “No,” she said. “I still believe most people are wrong about a great many things. Surely it's possible to be sane and believe that. After all, the greater part of the world has often had to change its opinion.”

Mrs. Cadwallader pursued the point no further with Dorothea, but told her husband, “It would be best if she married again as soon as decency permits, provided we could put her among the right people. Naturally the Chettams wouldn't like that. But plainly a husband is the best way to keep her in order. If we weren't so poor, I'd invite Lord Triton. He'll be a marquis one day, and there's no denying she'd make a fine marchioness. Mourning makes her look handsomer than ever.”
“My dear Elinor, leave the poor woman alone. These schemes do no good,” said the easygoing Rector.

“No good? How else do marriages happen, except by bringing men and women together? It's a disgrace that her uncle has run off and closed the Grange just now. Plenty of eligible men ought to be invited there and to Freshitt. Lord Triton is exactly right—full of rather muddle-headed plans to make people happy. He'd suit Mrs. Casaubon perfectly.”
“Let her make her own choice, Elinor.”

“That's the nonsense you wise men talk! How can she choose without a selection to choose from? A woman's choice generally means taking the only man available. Mark my words, Humphrey. Unless her friends make an effort, we'll have something worse than the Casaubon affair.”
“For heaven's sake, don't raise that subject, Elinor! It's extremely painful to Sir James. He'd be deeply offended if you mentioned it to him unnecessarily.”
“I haven't raised it,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, spreading her hands. “Celia told me everything about the will at the very beginning, without my asking.”
“Yes, yes. But they want it kept quiet. And I understand the young man is leaving the neighbourhood.”
Mrs. Cadwallader made no answer. She merely gave her husband three meaningful nods, her dark eyes filled with sarcasm.

Despite protests and persuasion, Dorothea quietly held to her decision. By the end of June all Lowick Manor's shutters stood open. Morning looked calmly into the library, lighting the rows of notebooks as it lights a desolate waste planted with enormous stones, the silent memorial of a forgotten faith. Evening, heavy with the scent of roses, entered the blue-green sitting room where Dorothea most often chose to sit. At first she went through every room, questioning the eighteen months of her marriage and continuing her thoughts as though speaking for her husband to hear. Then she lingered in the library. She could not rest until she had carefully arranged all the notebooks in the orderly sequence she imagined he would have wanted. The pity that had restrained and compelled her during their life together still clung to his image, even as she argued with him indignantly in her thoughts and told him he had been unjust. One small act may perhaps be smiled at as superstitious. She carefully enclosed and sealed the Synoptical Tabulation for the use of Mrs. Casaubon, writing inside the envelope: “I could not use it. Do you not see now that I could not submit my soul to yours by working without hope at something I do not believe in?—Dorothea.” Then she put the paper away in her own desk.

Perhaps that silent conversation was all the more earnest because beneath it, and running through it, lay the deep longing that had truly brought her back to Lowick. She wanted to see Will Ladislaw. She could imagine no good that a meeting would do. She was helpless; her hands were tied, preventing her from redressing any unfairness in his circumstances. Yet her soul thirsted for the sight of him. How could it be otherwise? Suppose, in the days of enchantment, a princess had seen some four-footed herd animal approach her repeatedly with a human gaze, singling her out in appeal. What would occupy her thoughts as she travelled? What would she seek when herds passed by? Surely the gaze that had found her, which she would recognize again. Life would be no better than tinsel by candlelight and rubbish by day if past experience did not move our spirits to longing and constancy. Dorothea truly did want to know the Farebrothers better, and especially to speak with the new Rector. But she also remembered Lydgate's account of Will and little Miss Noble, and counted on Will visiting the family at Lowick. On the first Sunday, _before_ entering the church, she saw him exactly where he had been on her previous visit, alone in the clergyman's pew. But _when_ she went inside, he had disappeared.
During weekday visits to the Rectory ladies, she listened in vain for some passing mention of Will. Mrs. Farebrother seemed to discuss everyone else, both within the neighbourhood and beyond it.

“I suppose some of Mr. Farebrother's Middlemarch congregation may come to hear him at Lowick occasionally. Don't you think so?” Dorothea asked, rather despising herself for the question's hidden motive.

“If they have any wisdom, they will, Mrs. Casaubon,” the old lady replied. “I see you properly appreciate my son's preaching. His grandfather on my side was an excellent clergyman. His father followed the law—an exemplary and honest man nevertheless, which explains why we never became rich. They call Fortune a woman, and a capricious one. But sometimes she's a good woman who gives to the deserving. That's what you've done, Mrs. Casaubon, by giving my son a living.”

Mrs. Farebrother returned to her knitting, dignifiedly satisfied with her neat little speech. But this was not what Dorothea had hoped to hear. Poor thing! She did not even know if Will Ladislaw was still in Middlemarch. There was nobody she dared ask, except perhaps Lydgate. Just now, however, seeing him would mean sending for him or going to find him. Perhaps Will had heard of Mr. Casaubon's strange prohibition against him and decided they had better never meet again. Perhaps she was wrong to want a meeting against which others might have many sound arguments. Yet after these sensible reflections, “But I do wish it” came as naturally as a sob after holding one's breath. The meeting did happen, though in a formal manner she had not expected.

One morning at about eleven, Dorothea sat in her private sitting room with a map of the manor's lands and other papers before her. She meant to use them to make an exact account of her income and affairs. She had not begun. Her hands lay folded in her lap while she looked along the lime avenue towards the distant fields. Every sunlit leaf was still. The familiar, unchanging view seemed an image of her future: a life of purposeless comfort—purposeless unless her own energy could discover reasons for passionate action. A widow's cap in those days framed the face in an oval, its crown rising above it; her dress demonstrated how much crape could possibly be applied. Yet this heavy solemnity of clothing only made her face look younger, with its restored colour and the sweet, questioning openness of her eyes.
Tantripp interrupted her thoughts. Mr. Ladislaw was downstairs, she said, requesting permission to see Madam if it was not too early.
“I'll see him,” Dorothea said, getting up at once. “Show him into the drawing room.”

For Dorothea, the drawing room was the house's most neutral space, least connected with the trials of her marriage. The damask matched the white-and-gold woodwork. Two tall mirrors stood there, and tables with nothing on them. In short, it was a room that gave you no reason to choose one seat over another. Beneath the sitting room, it too had a bow window overlooking the avenue. When Pratt showed Will in, however, the window was open. A winged visitor buzzed in and out occasionally, indifferent to the furniture, making the room seem less formal and deserted.
“It's good to see you here again, sir,” said Pratt, lingering to adjust a blind.
“I've only come to say goodbye, Pratt,” Will replied. Even the butler should know he was too proud to linger around Mrs. Casaubon now she was a wealthy widow.

“I'm very sorry to hear that, sir,” said Pratt as he withdrew. Naturally, being a servant who must be told nothing, he knew the fact still hidden from Ladislaw and had drawn his own conclusions. He had not disagreed with his fiancée Tantripp when she said, “Your master was jealous as a fiend, without any cause. Madam would look higher than Mr. Ladislaw, or I don't know her. Mrs. Cadwallader's maid says there's a lord coming to marry her when the mourning's over.”

Will had only a few moments to pace the room with his hat in his hand before Dorothea appeared. How different this was from their first meeting in Rome, when he had been embarrassed and she composed. Now he was miserable but determined, while her agitation could not be concealed. Just outside the door she had felt that this longed-for meeting was, after all, too difficult. As Will approached, a deep blush, rare for her, came with painful suddenness. Neither knew why, but neither spoke. She briefly offered her hand, then they sat near the window on facing settees. Will felt particularly uncomfortable. It seemed unlike Dorothea to receive him so differently merely because she was now a widow. He knew of no other change that could have affected their former relationship—except, as his imagination immediately suggested, that her friends might have been poisoning her mind with their suspicions.
“I hope I haven't presumed by calling,” Will said. “I couldn't bear to leave the neighbourhood and begin a new life without seeing you to say goodbye.”

“Presumed? Certainly not. I'd have thought it unkind if you hadn't wanted to see me,” said Dorothea. Her habit of complete sincerity asserted itself through all her uncertainty and distress. “Are you leaving straight away?”

“Very soon, I think. I mean to go to London and qualify for the bar by attending the required dinners. They say that's the preparation for every kind of public business. There'll soon be a great deal of political work, and I intend to try my hand at it. Other men have earned honourable positions without family influence or money.”

“That will only make it more honourable,” Dorothea said eagerly. “Besides, you have so many talents. My uncle has told me how well you speak in public—everyone's sorry when you finish—and how clearly you explain things. And you want justice for everyone. I'm so glad. In Rome I thought you cared only about poetry and art, the things that embellish life for those of us who are comfortably off. Now I know you think about everyone else as well.”
As she spoke, Dorothea's personal embarrassment faded. She became her former self again, looking straight at Will with delighted confidence.

“So you approve of my going away for years, and never returning until I've made some mark in the world?” Will asked. He was struggling to reconcile the utmost pride with an equally strong effort to draw some expression of deep feeling from her.

She did not realize how long she took to answer. Turning her head, she looked through the window at the rosebushes. They seemed to contain all the summers of the years Will would be gone. This was not prudent behaviour. But Dorothea never thought of calculating her manner; she thought only of submitting to the sad necessity that separated them. His first words about his plans had seemed to explain everything. She assumed he knew all about Mr. Casaubon's final action concerning him, and that the discovery had shocked him as it had shocked her. He had only ever felt friendship for her. Nothing in his mind had justified what she considered her husband's outrage against both their feelings. Yet his friendship remained. Something like a silent inward sob passed through Dorothea before she spoke. Her clear voice trembled at the last words, almost as though only from its own fluid flexibility.
“Yes, what you propose must be right. I'll be very happy to hear that people have recognized your worth. But you'll need patience. It may take a long time.”

Will could never quite explain how he stopped himself falling at her feet when she spoke that gently trembling “long time.” Afterwards he used to say that the dreadful colour and texture of her crape dress had probably restrained him. He remained seated, however, and said only—
“I'll never hear from you. And you'll forget me entirely.”

“No,” Dorothea replied, “I won't forget you. I've never forgotten anyone I once knew. My life has never been crowded, and I don't expect it will be. Besides, there's plenty of room for memories at Lowick, isn't there?” She smiled.

“Good God!” Will exclaimed passionately. Still holding his hat, he rose and walked to a marble table, suddenly turning to lean his back against it. Colour flooded his face and neck; he looked almost angry. He felt as though they were two creatures slowly turning into marble before one another, their hearts still conscious and their eyes still longing. But nothing could be done. He would never allow it to be said that he had come to this meeting with bitter determination only to end by confessing feelings that could be interpreted as a request for her fortune. Moreover, he really feared the effect such a confession might have on Dorothea herself.

From across the room she watched him uneasily, wondering if her words had offended him. Meanwhile her thoughts kept returning to his probable lack of money and her inability to help. Had her uncle been home, she might have done something through him! Her preoccupation with the hardship of Will's poverty, while she possessed what should have been his share, led her to speak again as he remained silent, looking away.
“I wonder whether you'd like the miniature hanging upstairs—I mean that lovely portrait of your grandmother. If you'd like it, I don't think I ought to keep it. It looks remarkably like you.”
“That's very kind,” Will said irritably. “No, I don't particularly want it. Owning one's own likeness isn't much consolation. It would be more comforting if someone else wanted it.”
“I thought you'd want to cherish her memory. I thought—” Dorothea stopped briefly, her imagination warning her away from Aunt Julia's history. “Surely you'd like the miniature as a family keepsake.”
“Why should I have that when I've nothing else? A man whose only storage is a portmanteau has to keep his memories in his head.”

Will spoke without thinking, simply releasing his irritation. Being offered his grandmother's portrait at that moment was a little too exasperating. But Dorothea found a particular sting in his words. She stood and answered with a trace of both indignation and pride.
“Having nothing makes you much the happier of the two of us, Mr. Ladislaw.”

Will was taken aback. Whatever she meant, her tone sounded like a dismissal. He stopped leaning against the table and moved a little towards her. Their eyes met with a strange, questioning seriousness. Something kept their minds apart, leaving each to guess the other's thoughts. Will had never really considered himself entitled to inherit any of the property Dorothea now held. He would have needed the whole story explained to understand what she was feeling.
“Until now, I've never thought having nothing a misfortune,” he said. “But poverty can be as bad as leprosy if it separates us from what we care for most.”
The words pierced Dorothea's heart and softened her. She answered with the sadness of someone who understood.

“Sorrow reaches us in so many ways. Two years ago I didn't understand that—the unexpected ways trouble comes, tying our hands and silencing us when we're longing to speak. I used to feel rather contemptuous of women for not shaping their lives more, for not doing better things. I was very fond of having my own way. I've almost given that up,” she finished with a playful smile.

“I haven't given up doing what I want, but I very rarely can,” said Will. He stood two yards away, his mind crowded with conflicting wishes and resolutions. He longed for unmistakable proof that she loved him, yet dreaded the position such proof might put him in. “What we want most may come with conditions we couldn't possibly bear.”
Just then Pratt came in. “Sir James Chettam is in the library, madam.”

“Ask him to come here,” Dorothea said at once. It was as though one electric shock had passed through both her and Will. Each felt a proud defiance. Neither looked at the other as they waited for Sir James.
After shaking Dorothea's hand, Sir James gave Ladislaw the slightest possible bow. Will returned it with precisely equal coldness. Then he approached Dorothea and said—
“I must say goodbye, Mrs. Casaubon. Probably for a long time.”

Dorothea held out her hand and said goodbye warmly. Sensing that Sir James was treating Will as an inferior and behaving rudely, she felt her resolution and dignity rise. There was no embarrassment in her manner. After Will left, she turned to Sir James with such calm composure and asked, “How is Celia?” that he had to act as though nothing had displeased him. What would any other behaviour achieve? Indeed, Sir James disliked so intensely even the thought of Dorothea and Ladislaw as possible lovers that he wished to avoid any display of irritation acknowledging the possibility. Asked why he recoiled so strongly, he might at first have offered nothing fuller or more precise than “_That_ Ladislaw!” On reflection, he might have argued that Mr. Casaubon's codicil, penalizing a marriage between them, made any relationship whatsoever inappropriate. His aversion grew stronger because he felt powerless to intervene.
Yet Sir James exerted an influence he never suspected. By arriving at that moment, he embodied the strongest reasons that made Will's pride a force of resistance, holding him apart from Dorothea.
